questions.stem: Determine the enzyme that is competitively inhibited by statin drugs.
questions.why: Statins occupy the substrate-binding site of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) reductase. By competing with HMG-CoA, they reduce mevalonate production and slow cholesterol synthesis in the liver.

notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase can phosphorylate and inhibit the reductase when cellular energy is scarce.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, placing it a step removed from the enzyme that binds statins.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes an inhibitory phosphate from the reductase, restoring its activity independently of statin binding.
notes.E: Protein kinase A transmits signals from cyclic AMP, whereas statins bind the enzyme that produces mevalonate.

questions.stem: Which of these enzymes deactivates HMG-CoA Reductase?
questions.why: When cellular energy is scarce, AMP-activated protein kinase phosphorylates HMG-CoA reductase. This reduces the production of mevalonate and slows the energy-consuming synthesis of cholesterol.

notes.A: The reductase converts HMG-CoA into mevalonate and receives its inhibitory phosphate from a separate kinase.
notes.C: An upstream kinase activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which then directly phosphorylates the reductase.
notes.D: The phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphate from HMG-CoA reductase, allowing cholesterol synthesis to resume.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas the enzyme that directly senses energy status and inhibits the reductase is AMP-activated protein kinase.

questions.stem: Which enzyme activates AMP activated kinase?
questions.why: An upstream kinase phosphorylates a threonine in the catalytic subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase. This phosphorylation allows the energy sensor to inhibit biosynthetic pathways when energy is scarce.

notes.A: HMG-CoA reductase makes mevalonate and is a downstream target of the activated energy sensor.
notes.B: AMP-activated protein kinase is the enzyme receiving the activating phosphate in this signalling step.
notes.D: The reductase phosphatase restores the activity of the cholesterol-synthesis enzyme by removing its inhibitory phosphate.
notes.E: Protein kinase A responds to cyclic AMP, whereas a distinct upstream kinase phosphorylates the activation loop of the energy sensor.

questions.stem: cAMP indirectly deactivates HMG-CoA Reductase, through which protein is this effect mediated?
questions.why: Glucagon/epinephrine increases cAMP, which activates PKA. PKA initiates a cascade that keeps HMG-CoA reductase phosphorylated and inactive.

notes.A: The reductase is the target being inactivated, not the mediator.
notes.B: AMPK responds to low energy (AMP), not to cAMP.
notes.C: AMPK kinase is not activated by cAMP.
notes.D: The phosphatase is what PKA switches off; it does not carry the cAMP signal itself.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting step in fatty acid synthesis is:

options.label: C
options.text: formation of malonyl-CoA from malonate and coenzyme A.

options.label: D
options.text: the reaction catalyzed by acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

options.label: E
options.text: the reduction of the acetoacetyl group to a β-hydroxybutyryl group

questions.why: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase uses ATP, bicarbonate and the cofactor biotin to convert acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. This commits carbon to fatty acid synthesis and controls the supply of two-carbon units for elongation.

notes.A: Condensation takes place on fatty acid synthase once the carboxylase has supplied the malonyl group.
notes.B: Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA, but this also supplies pathways other than fatty acid synthesis.
notes.C: The carboxylase adds bicarbonate-derived carbon to acetyl-CoA, so free malonate is not its starting material.
notes.E: The first reduction on fatty acid synthase consumes NADPH after the chain has already undergone condensation.

questions.stem: The biosynthesis of triacylglycerols from acetate occurs mainly in:

options.label: B
options.text: humans after ingestion of excess carbohydrate.

questions.why: A sustained carbohydrate surplus can provide acetyl-CoA for new fatty acids and glycerol 3-phosphate for their storage as triacylglycerol. Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and esterification in the fed state.

notes.A: Plants also synthesise triacylglycerols, which are an important energy reserve in many seeds.
notes.C: Low carbohydrate availability generally favours oxidation of fatty acids and reduces the use of carbohydrate carbon for new fatty acids.
notes.D: Animals synthesise triacylglycerols in the fed state, including in the liver and adipose tissue.
notes.E: A sustained carbohydrate surplus supplies both carbon and an insulin signal for fat storage in humans.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about triacylglycerol synthesis is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Humans can store more energy in glycogen than in triacylglycerols.

options.label: B
options.text: Insulin stimulates conversion of dietary carbohydrate into triacylglycerols.

options.label: C
options.text: It is not a hormone-sensitive process.

options.label: D
options.text: Mammals are unable to convert carbohydrates into triacylglycerols.

options.label: E
options.text: Phosphatidate is not on the pathway of triacylglycerol synthesis.

questions.why: Insulin favours storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal. Glucose supplies glycerol 3-phosphate for the triacylglycerol backbone and can supply acetyl-CoA for synthesis of the attached fatty acids.

notes.A: Fat is stored with little water and yields more energy per gram than hydrated glycogen.
notes.C: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage after feeding, while low insulin favours release of fatty acids from adipose tissue.
notes.D: Mammalian liver can convert surplus glucose into fatty acids and esterify these to form triacylglycerols.
notes.E: Phosphatidate loses its phosphate to form diacylglycerol, which receives a third fatty acyl group.

questions.stem: A strategy that is not employed in the synthesis of phospholipids is:

options.label: D
options.text: exchange of free alcohol with head group alcohol of phospholipid.

options.label: E
options.text: remodeling of head group alcohols by chemical modification

questions.why: In the cytidine diphosphate (CDP) routes, one partner is activated and the other supplies a free hydroxyl group. Linking two CDP-activated partners is unnecessary for forming the phosphodiester bond.

notes.A: CDP-choline transfers its phosphocholine group to diacylglycerol during the formation of phosphatidylcholine.
notes.B: Free inositol reacts with activated CDP-diacylglycerol in the pathway that forms phosphatidylinositol.
notes.D: Mammalian cells can exchange serine for the ethanolamine head group of phosphatidylethanolamine to make phosphatidylserine.
notes.E: The liver can synthesise phosphatidylcholine by adding three methyl groups to the head group of phosphatidylethanolamine.

questions.stem: The major source of cholesterol in arterial smooth muscle cells is from:
questions.why: Low-density lipoprotein carries much of the cholesterol in plasma as cholesteryl esters. Cells can bind its apolipoprotein B-100 through LDL receptors and take up the particle by endocytosis.

notes.A: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is a remnant that can return to the liver or give rise to low-density lipoprotein.
notes.C: High-density lipoprotein accepts excess cholesterol from peripheral cells and participates in its return to the liver.
notes.D: Chylomicrons chiefly deliver dietary triacylglycerol, and their cholesterol-rich remnants are taken up by the liver.
notes.E: Very-low-density lipoprotein chiefly exports hepatic triacylglycerol and gives rise to cholesterol-enriched particles as it loses fat.

questions.stem: Endogenous triglycerides in plasma is maximally bound to:
questions.why: The liver packages triacylglycerol into very-low-density lipoprotein for export. Lipoprotein lipase then hydrolyses the particle's triacylglycerol in capillaries, making fatty acids available to muscle and adipose tissue.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are rich in triacylglycerol too, but the intestine produces them to transport fat absorbed from a meal.
notes.B: Low-density lipoprotein has already lost much of its precursor's triacylglycerol and is enriched in cholesteryl esters.
notes.D: High-density lipoprotein participates mainly in cholesterol transport and carries a relatively small amount of triacylglycerol.
notes.E: Intermediate-density lipoprotein is the remnant formed after lipoprotein lipase has removed some triacylglycerol from the hepatic particle.

questions.stem: The precursor of cholesterol synthesis is:
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA supplies all the carbon atoms retained in cholesterol. Its two-carbon units first form acetoacetyl-CoA and then HMG-CoA, which is reduced to mevalonate in the sterol pathway.

notes.A: Free acetate must first be activated with coenzyme A before it can enter cholesterol synthesis.
notes.C: Oxaloacetate can help export acetyl units as citrate, but is regenerated when cytosolic citrate is cleaved.
notes.D: Malate participates in the citrate shuttle and can help supply reducing power for biosynthesis.
notes.E: Pyruvate can yield acetyl-CoA through oxidative decarboxylation, placing it upstream of the direct building block.

questions.stem: All are derived of cholesterol except:
questions.why: Cholecystokinin is made by intestinal endocrine cells from a peptide precursor, preprocholecystokinin. The other choices are sterols or products of sterol metabolism.

notes.A: The liver oxidises and shortens the side chain of cholesterol to form primary bile acids, including chenodeoxycholic acid.
notes.B: Glycocholic acid forms when the liver conjugates the cholesterol-derived bile acid cholic acid with glycine.
notes.C: Steroid-producing cells convert cholesterol to pregnenolone, from which they can synthesise testosterone.
notes.D: In skin, ultraviolet B light acts on the sterol precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol to initiate vitamin D₃ synthesis.

questions.stem: Determine the lipoprotein that best detect Lipid profile of a non-fasting patient:
questions.why: Non-fasting blood primarily reflects the presence of dietary chylomicrons.

notes.A: LDL changes little after a meal.
notes.B: VLDL is mainly of liver origin and changes little soon after a meal.
notes.D: IDL is a VLDL remnant and is not meal-dependent.
notes.E: Total cholesterol is not a lipoprotein and changes little after a meal.

questions.stem: Clinically, bile acids are important in:

options.label: B
options.text: enhancing the formation of atherogenic plaques

options.label: C
options.text: inhibition of intestinal absorption of fat soluble vitamins

questions.why: Converting cholesterol to bile acids and excreting them in faeces is the body's main route for getting rid of excess cholesterol (sterol). Bile acids emulsify fats; they do not precipitate them, they do not promote plaques, they are needed FOR fat-soluble vitamin absorption, and they do not cause fatty liver.

notes.A: Bile acids emulsify fats; they do not precipitate them.
notes.B: Bile acid loss lowers cholesterol, so it opposes plaque formation.
notes.C: Bile acids are needed FOR fat-soluble vitamin absorption.
notes.D: Bile acids do not cause fatty liver.

questions.stem: A person with a type IIA hyperlipoproteinemia had a blood cholesterol level of 360 mg/dL and blood triglyceride levels of 140 mg/dL. This person most likely has:

options.label: A
options.text: an increased ability to produce VLDL

options.label: B
options.text: a decreased ability for receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL

options.label: C
options.text: an elevation of HDL in the blood

options.label: D
options.text: a decreased ability to convert VLDL to IDL

questions.why: Type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia is an isolated elevation of LDL with relatively normal triglycerides. Reduced receptor-mediated LDL clearance is a classic cause, as in familial hypercholesterolaemia due to an impaired LDL receptor pathway.

notes.A: Increased hepatic production of VLDL would usually raise plasma triglycerides rather than producing an isolated increase in LDL cholesterol.
notes.C: High HDL does not explain an isolated accumulation of LDL particles in type IIa hyperlipoproteinaemia.
notes.D: Impaired processing of VLDL would retain more triglyceride-rich particles. It is not the expected mechanism for an isolated LDL elevation.

questions.stem: A person with a low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor deficiency was treated with lovastatin. As a consequence of the action of this drug, the person should have:

options.label: A
options.text: fewer LDL receptors in cell membranes

questions.why: Lovastatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase and decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis. Lower intracellular cholesterol can increase expression of functioning LDL receptors, increasing LDL clearance and lowering blood cholesterol. The response is smaller when receptor activity is nearly absent.

notes.A: Lower hepatic cholesterol generally increases expression of residual functional LDL receptors through sterol-sensitive regulation.
notes.B: Lovastatin decreases de novo cholesterol synthesis by competitively inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, even though feedback can increase enzyme expression.
notes.C: ACAT esterifies intracellular cholesterol for storage. Increased esterification is not the principal action of lovastatin.
notes.E: Statins usually lower LDL and can also modestly decrease circulating triglyceride concentrations rather than raising them.

questions.stem: Arrange the following lipoproteins in increasing order of density:
questions.why: Lipoprotein density increases as the fraction of protein relative to lipid increases. The order from lowest to highest is chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL. The proposed sequences do not follow that order.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are the least dense, but VLDL is less dense than LDL and must come before LDL.
notes.B: HDL has the highest density in this group and follows LDL in the order of increasing density.
notes.C: VLDL is less dense than IDL, because IDL is a smaller remnant left after some triglyceride has been removed.
notes.D: HDL, LDL and VLDL are listed in descending rather than ascending order of density.

questions.stem:
During fatty acid synthesis, the growing acyl chain is covalently attached to which of the following? Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: The growing chain is held as a thioester on the acyl carrier protein arms (the pantetheinyl -SH of ACP and the cysteinyl -SH of the condensing enzyme, called ACP1 and ACP2 in this course). NADPH and the reductases act on the chain but do not carry it.

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out IV, which is true.
notes.B: Includes I and II, which are false, and leaves out IV, which is true.
notes.C: Includes I and III, which are false, and leaves out IV, which is true.
notes.E: Includes I, II and III, which are false, and leaves out IV, which is true.

questions.stem: Transfers Acetyl group from CoA to cysteinyl-S on ACP.
questions.why: Acetyl-CoA: ACP transacylase transfers the acetyl group from Coenzyme A to the active site of the ACP.

notes.A: NADPH is a reducing agent, not a transferase.
notes.B: ACP is the carrier, not the enzyme that loads it.
notes.C: ACP is the carrier, not the enzyme that loads it.
notes.D: The reductase reduces the β-keto group; it does not transfer acetyl groups.

questions.stem: Transfers Malonyl group from CoA to pantetheinyl-S on ACP.
questions.why: The malonyl/acetyltransferase domain of mammalian fatty acid synthase transfers malonyl from malonyl-CoA to the terminal thiol of ACP's phosphopantetheine arm. The loaded malonyl–ACP supplies a two-carbon unit during condensation.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents for later steps. It does not transfer the malonyl group from CoA.
notes.B: An acyl carrier protein holds the malonyl group as a thioester. The transfer reaction is catalysed by the transferase domain.
notes.C: The mobile ACP arm carries substrates between enzyme sites. Catalysis of malonyl loading requires the distinct transacylase activity.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase uses NADPH after condensation to reduce a carbonyl group. It does not load malonyl onto ACP.

questions.stem: In this reaction CO2 departs from malonylCoA reducing ACP. Which enzyme catalyzes this?
questions.why: The condensation reaction joins the acetyl and malonyl groups, decarboxylating the malonyl group to release CO2. This is catalyzed by Keto Acyl: ACP synthase.

notes.A: ACP is a carrier, not an enzyme.
notes.B: ACP is a carrier, not an enzyme.
notes.C: The transacylase only loads malonyl onto ACP.
notes.E: Thioesterase releases the finished palmitate.

questions.stem:
Reduction of the keto group to an alcohol requires: Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: After condensation, beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce the beta-keto group to a hydroxyl group. This is the first reduction in the fatty acid synthase elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH supplies reducing equivalents, but the reduction also requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase to catalyse hydride transfer.
notes.C: Enoyl–ACP reductase acts later on the carbon–carbon double bond. The keto group requires beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase.
notes.D: ACP carries the intermediate but is neither the reductase nor the reducing cofactor for the keto group.
notes.E: The cycle has two reduction reactions. The later enoyl reductase is not needed for the initial conversion of the keto group to an alcohol.

questions.stem:
The enoyl group is reduced to a saturated group by: Key:
I. NADPH
II. β-keto-acyl:ACP reductase
III. enoyl-ACP reductase
IV. ACP1 and ACP2
V. ACP-acyl transferase
questions.why: After dehydration makes a trans-enoyl–ACP intermediate, enoyl–ACP reductase uses NADPH to reduce its carbon–carbon double bond. This yields a saturated acyl–ACP ready for another elongation cycle.

notes.A: NADPH donates reducing equivalents, but the enoyl reductase is required to transfer them to the double bond.
notes.B: Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts earlier on the carbonyl group, before dehydration produces the enoyl intermediate.
notes.D: ACP can hold the enoyl intermediate, but it does not supply reducing equivalents or replace enoyl–ACP reductase.
notes.E: Both reductases use NADPH in the overall cycle. Beta-ketoacyl–ACP reductase acts at a separate earlier step.

questions.stem: Most potent reducing agent in fatty acid synthesis:
questions.why: NADPH provides the reducing equivalents for both reductive steps of mammalian fatty acid synthesis. One NADPH reduces the beta-keto group and another reduces the double bond in each elongation cycle.

notes.B: An acyl carrier protein binds and carries growing intermediates. It does not donate the electrons required for reduction.
notes.C: An ACP domain is a carrier with a phosphopantetheine arm, rather than the source of reducing equivalents.
notes.D: The beta-ketoacyl reductase catalyses reduction but obtains the reducing equivalents it transfers from NADPH.
notes.E: The transacylase loads acetyl and malonyl groups. It is not the source of reducing equivalents.

questions.stem: What constitutes the substrate-carrying arm of the synthase complex:
questions.why: The Acyl Carrier Protein (ACP) holds the growing fatty acid chain during synthesis.

notes.B: ACP II is not the substrate-carrying arm in this scheme.
notes.C: The transferase is an enzyme that loads the arm, not the arm itself.
notes.D: Thioesterase releases the product.
notes.E: NADPH is the reductant, not a carrier.

questions.stem: Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase may not give rise to the following clinical manifestation:
questions.why: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes hypertriglyceridemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and xanthomas, but not muscular dystrophy.

notes.A: Hepatosplenomegaly IS a feature, from lipid-laden macrophages.
notes.B: Abdominal pain IS a feature (pancreatitis from very high chylomicrons).
notes.C: Eruptive xanthomata ARE a feature.
notes.D: Lack of lipase activity in post-heparin plasma IS the diagnostic finding.

questions.stem: Type III hyperlipidemia is caused by a deficiency in apoprotein E. Analysis of the serum of patient with this disorder would exhibit which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: An absence of chylomicrons after eating

options.label: B
options.text: Normal levels of VLDL after eating

questions.why: Type III hyperlipoproteinaemia is caused by defective clearance of cholesterol-rich remnants, often associated with an apoE variant such as apoE2. The accumulated remnant particles carry both triglyceride and cholesterol, so both can be elevated.

notes.A: The intestine can still make chylomicrons after eating. The defect involves clearance of remnant particles rather than absence of chylomicron production.
notes.B: Remnants derived from VLDL can accumulate, so normal VLDL-related lipid handling is not typical of the disorder.
notes.C: Retained triglyceride-rich remnants contribute to elevated triglyceride levels rather than an isolated normal triglyceride result.
notes.D: Cholesterol carried in accumulating remnant particles is often elevated, along with triglycerides.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the fatty acid elongation system of vertebrate cells?

options.label: A
options.text: It involves the same four-step sequence seen in the fatty acid synthase complex.

options.label: B
options.text: It is located in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

options.label: C
options.text: It produces stearoyl-CoA by the extension of palmitoyl-CoA.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses malonyl-CoA as a substrate.

options.label: E
options.text: The immediate precursor of the added carbons is acetyl-CoA.

questions.why: In the principal endoplasmic-reticulum elongation system, malonyl-CoA is the immediate donor of the two carbons added to the acyl chain. Acetyl-CoA is upstream as a source of malonyl-CoA, rather than the immediate donor in the elongase reaction.

notes.A: Each elongation round uses condensation, reduction, dehydration and a second reduction, analogous to the sequence of fatty acid synthase.
notes.B: The major elongase system for long-chain acyl-CoAs is associated with the endoplasmic reticulum.
notes.C: One elongation round can convert a 16-carbon palmitoyl-CoA to an 18-carbon product, stearoyl-CoA.
notes.D: Malonyl-CoA is a substrate for the endoplasmic-reticulum elongase and supplies the added carbons after decarboxylation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the differences between fatty acid synthesis and fatty acid β-oxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: A thioester derivative of crotonic acid (trans-2-butenoic acid) is an intermediate in the synthetic path, but not in the degradative path.

options.label: B
options.text: A thioester derivative of D-β-hydroxybutyrate is an intermediate in the synthetic path, not in the degradative path.

options.label: C
options.text: Fatty acid synthesis uses NADPH, whereas β-oxidation produces NADH and FADH2.

options.label: D
options.text: Fatty acid degradation is catalysed by cytosolic enzymes; fatty acid synthesis by mitochondrial enzymes.

options.label: E
options.text: The condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules in a crude extract is faster in bicarbonate buffer than in phosphate buffer at the same pH.

questions.why: It is the reverse: fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic and β-oxidation is mitochondrial. The other statements are true (synthesis uses the D-isomer and NADPH; bicarbonate is needed for acetyl-CoA carboxylase).

notes.A: True: crotonyl-ACP is a synthetic intermediate; β-oxidation uses the CoA form.
notes.B: True: synthesis uses the D-isomer, β-oxidation the L-isomer.
notes.C: True: this is a real difference between the two paths.
notes.E: True: bicarbonate supplies CO2 for acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.stem: A healthy 70-year-old man is told to fast for 12 hours before his plasma lipids are measured, but he eats a large breakfast 3 hours before the blood draw. Which change is most likely?
questions.why: A large meal supplies triglyceride that enterocytes package into chylomicrons. At about three hours after eating, these triglyceride-rich particles can increase circulating triglycerides. LDL and HDL cholesterol usually change less acutely.

notes.B: Postprandial dietary lipid is carried mainly in chylomicrons. A sharp immediate rise in LDL cholesterol is not the characteristic effect.
notes.C: HDL cholesterol usually does not fall sharply after a single meal in a healthy person. Triglyceride-rich particles change more.
notes.D: VLDL is produced in the liver, while the new postprandial particles come from the intestine. A sharp fall in VLDL is not the expected change.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Friedewald equation is considered fairly accurate and widely employed.
Reason: some factors that could cause deviations in the Friedewald equation are unaccounted for using this calculation.
questions.why: The Friedewald equation has long been used to estimate LDL cholesterol and can work reasonably in appropriate samples. Its simplifying assumptions can cause error at high triglyceride concentrations or very low LDL. Those limitations do not explain its widespread use.

notes.A: Both statements can be true, but the unmodelled factors explain potential error rather than why the calculation is useful.
notes.C: The equation has practical limitations because the triglyceride-to-cholesterol ratio in VLDL is not constant across samples.
notes.D: The long-standing use of the estimate in appropriate settings is real, even though newer equations can improve accuracy.
notes.E: The estimate is widely used historically, and the concern about unaccounted sources of error is also valid.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Hypertriglyceridemia may lead to Pancreatitis.
Reason: excessively elevated levels of chylomicrons from diet can cause occlusion of the capillaries leading to ischaemia and local acidaemia which can expose triglycerides to pancreatic lipases whose effect is the degradation of triglycerides to free fatty acids, causing to cytotoxic injury.
questions.why: Very high triglycerides can cause acute pancreatitis. A proposed mechanism is that chylomicron-rich blood impairs pancreatic microcirculation and lipases release locally injurious free fatty acids. Ischaemia and local acidosis can reinforce the injury.

notes.B: The reason provides a recognised mechanism that can connect severe triglyceride elevation to pancreatic tissue injury.
notes.C: Capillary flow changes and free-fatty-acid toxicity are plausible contributors to the link, even though they may not account for every case.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia is an established cause of acute pancreatitis, so the assertion is not false.
notes.E: Both the association and the proposed microvascular and lipotoxic explanation have physiological support.

questions.stem: Enzymes that catalyze the synthesis of long chain fatty acids in vertebrate cells:

options.label: C
options.text: are localized in the mitochondrial matrix.

options.label: D
options.text: are part of a single polypeptide chain containing several distinct enzyme activities.

options.label: E
options.text: have none of the characteristics above.

questions.why: Vertebrate cytosolic fatty acid synthase is a type I synthase. Each polypeptide contains multiple catalytic domains and an ACP domain, and two polypeptides associate to form the functional complex that commonly produces palmitate.

notes.A: Separate proteins carry out the individual reactions of type II synthase systems. The vertebrate cytosolic enzyme combines the activities in one polypeptide.
notes.B: Cytosolic fatty acid synthase is encoded by a nuclear gene, rather than by the mitochondrial genome.
notes.C: The major pathway for de novo palmitate production is cytosolic. Mitochondria have a distinct specialised synthesis system.
notes.E: Multiple enzyme activities assembled in one protein chain are a defining feature of the vertebrate type I synthase.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true of the fatty acid synthesis and the fatty acid β-oxidation systems?

options.label: A
options.text: A derivative of the vitamin pantothenic acid is involved.

options.label: C
options.text: Double bonds are oxidized or reduced by pyridine nucleotide coenzymes.

options.label: D
options.text: The processes occur in different cellular compartments.

options.label: E
options.text: The processes occur in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.why: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol; only beta-oxidation occurs in the mitochondria.

notes.A: Both use a pantothenate derivative (CoA, and the ACP arm).
notes.B: Acyl-CoA (or acyl-ACP) derivatives are intermediates in both.
notes.C: NAD(P) reduces or oxidises the double bonds in both.
notes.D: True: synthesis is cytosolic and β-oxidation mitochondrial.

questions.stem: HMG CoA reductase is inhibited by:
questions.why: Lovastatin is a statin. Its active form competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing mevalonate formation and hepatic cholesterol synthesis.

notes.A: Clofibrate is a fibrate that acts mainly through PPAR-alpha to change expression of lipid metabolism genes.
notes.B: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate used to lower triglycerides. Its principal mechanism does not involve direct inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase.
notes.D: Cholestyramine binds bile acids in the gut and increases their faecal loss. It does not directly inhibit the reductase.
notes.E: Lovastatin has a well-defined direct inhibitory action at the reductase substrate-binding site.

questions.stem: Atherosclerosis can be managed by the following drug treatment:
questions.why: Simvastatin inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase, which lowers intracellular cholesterol and increases LDL receptor expression. The resulting decline in circulating LDL reduces the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular events.

notes.A: Low-dose niacin is not standard drug therapy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk reduction. Lipid effects from pharmacological niacin do not substitute for established statin benefit.
notes.B: High-dose vitamin C is not an established substitute for LDL-lowering therapy to reduce atherosclerotic events.
notes.C: Bariatric surgery can improve some cardiovascular risk factors in selected patients, but it is a procedure rather than the drug treatment asked for.
notes.D: Dietary modification contributes to risk reduction. It is a lifestyle intervention rather than a medication.

questions.stem: Atherosclerotic plaques development cannot be accelerated under the following pathological conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: The consumption of high fat diets

questions.why: HDL is cardioprotective and prevents plaque formation.

notes.A: A high-fat diet raises LDL and speeds up plaque formation.
notes.B: Oxidised LDL is taken up by macrophages to form foam cells.
notes.C: Small dense LDL is highly atherogenic.
notes.E: High LDL in familial hypercholesterolaemia speeds up plaque formation.

questions.stem: The clinical importance of apolipoproteins:

options.label: A
options.text: Solubilization of lipids in the gut

options.label: C
options.text: Can inactivate some lipid metabolic enzymes

options.label: D
options.text: Prevents the cholestasis of bile salts

questions.why: ApoB-100 and ApoE act as ligands for receptors.

notes.A: Bile salts solubilise lipids in the gut, not apolipoproteins.
notes.C: Apolipoproteins mainly ACTIVATE enzymes (e.g. C-II for lipoprotein lipase).
notes.D: Cholestasis is not prevented by apolipoproteins.
notes.E: Lipidoses are lysosomal enzyme defects, not apolipoprotein disorders.

questions.stem: Which apoprotein is the main structural protein of VLDL?
questions.why: Liver-derived VLDL contains one apoB-100 molecule per particle. ApoB-100 is the structural scaffold and remains with the particle as it is converted to IDL and, for some particles, LDL.

notes.B: ApoB-48 is a shorter product expressed in the intestine and is the structural protein of chylomicrons.
notes.C: ApoA-I is the principal structural apolipoprotein of HDL, rather than the scaffold of VLDL.
notes.D: ApoC-II can be carried on VLDL and activates lipoprotein lipase. It is exchangeable and not the main structural protein.
notes.E: ApoE helps hepatic receptors recognise some triglyceride-rich remnants. It is not the fixed structural scaffold of VLDL.

questions.stem: The most important long-term clinical consequence of persistently raised plasma VLDL is:
questions.why: Persistently elevated VLDL can increase exposure to atherogenic apoB-containing remnant particles. Smaller VLDL remnants can enter and be retained in the arterial wall, contributing to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

notes.B: VLDL and its remnants carry cholesterol as well as triglyceride. Persistent elevation does not characteristically cause low blood cholesterol.
notes.C: Hepatosplenomegaly can occur in severe chylomicronaemia or other disorders. It is not the principal long-term consequence of chronically raised VLDL.
notes.D: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia can cause abdominal pain from pancreatitis. Atherosclerosis is the key long-term vascular consequence of increased atherogenic remnants.
notes.E: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency can cause triglyceride-rich particles to accumulate. It is a possible underlying disorder, rather than a consequence of increased VLDL.

questions.stem: Lipidoses:

options.label: A
options.text: are acquired diseases of catabolism of lipids

options.label: B
options.text: there is deficiency of the respective lipid substrate in the nervous system and/or peripheral tissues

options.label: C
options.text: there is accumulation of lipid substrate in the stomach resulting in obesity

options.label: D
options.text: the clinical chemical diagnosis can be accomplished by demonstration of the enzyme defect

options.label: E
options.text: the clinical chemical diagnosis cannot be accomplished by the demonstration of substrate accumulation in body fluids

questions.why: Many lipidoses are inherited storage disorders in which a defect in lipid degradation causes particular substrates to accumulate. Demonstration of reduced activity of the relevant enzyme can support the diagnosis, sometimes together with genetic and biomarker tests.

notes.A: Classic lipid storage disorders are usually inherited rather than acquired during life.
notes.B: The substrate typically accumulates because it cannot be degraded normally. Its concentration may rise in affected tissue rather than fall.
notes.C: These disorders can affect nervous tissue, liver and other organs. They do not generally cause ordinary obesity by lipid accumulation in the stomach.
notes.E: Some accumulated lipids or derivatives can be detected in body fluids and serve as useful biomarkers, depending on the disorder.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of drugs regulating Familial hypercholestolaemia:

options.label: A
options.text: Cholestyramine: combines with bile acids and prevent cholesterol reabsorption

options.label: B
options.text: Cholestyramine: combines with lipoprotein lipase and prevent cholesterol reabsorption

options.label: C
options.text: Small doses of niacin prevent cholesterol absorption

options.label: D
options.text: Large doses of niacin prevent cholesterol excretion

questions.why: Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant.

notes.B: Cholestyramine binds bile acids, not an enzyme.
notes.C: Niacin works only at high doses.
notes.D: Niacin reduces VLDL production; it does not block cholesterol excretion.
notes.E: Sitosterol competes with dietary cholesterol for absorption.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a mild heart attack and is placed on diet and statin therapy. What will be the most likely result of this therapy?
questions.why: Statins lower hepatic cholesterol synthesis and increase expression of functioning hepatic LDL receptors. This increases clearance of circulating LDL and usually lowers LDL cholesterol during treatment.

notes.A: A rise in total blood cholesterol is not the expected response when the major LDL cholesterol fraction is being lowered.
notes.B: Statins act chiefly on cholesterol synthesis and LDL clearance, not by lowering blood glucose.
notes.D: Fatty acid beta-oxidation is a separate pathway. Reduced oxidation is not the usual marker of an effective statin response.
notes.E: Hepatic LDL uptake normally increases during statin treatment, so circulating LDL tends to fall rather than rise.

questions.stem: Type I hyperlipidemia may be caused by a deficiency of apoprotein C-II. What would be exhibited by analysis of the serum of patients with this disorder?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher than normal levels of VLDL after eating

questions.why: ApoC-II normally activates lipoprotein lipase. When apoC-II is deficient, triglycerides in chylomicrons are cleared poorly, producing severe hypertriglyceridaemia. This can resemble inherited lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

notes.A: Type I hyperlipoproteinaemia is defined primarily by accumulation of chylomicrons rather than an isolated postprandial increase in VLDL.
notes.B: Failure to activate lipoprotein lipase impairs removal of circulating triglyceride, so a normal triglyceride level is not the expected hallmark.
notes.D: Chylomicrons carry some cholesterol, but the most characteristic change is a major elevation of triglycerides.
notes.E: Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity decreases triglyceride clearance, so triglyceride-rich particles remain in plasma.

questions.stem: Lipoprotein particle metabolism can occur:

options.label: A
options.text: via the exogenous or endogenous pathway,

options.label: B
options.text: Independent of the source of origin.

questions.why: Lipoproteins are metabolized via exogenous (dietary) and endogenous (hepatic) pathways.

notes.B: The pathway depends on whether the lipid is dietary or made in the liver.
notes.C: Bile is needed to absorb dietary lipid.
notes.D: Lipoproteins are also processed in the intestine, plasma and tissues.

questions.stem: Lipoproteins are characterized based on their various proportions which determine their by their density. Which one of the following sequences places the lipoproteins in the order of most dense to least dense?
questions.why: HDL is richest in protein relative to lipid and has the greatest density among these particles. The density then decreases through LDL and VLDL, with triglyceride-rich chylomicrons least dense.

notes.A: LDL is denser than VLDL and must precede it when the particles are listed from most to least dense.
notes.C: HDL has greater density than LDL and chylomicrons, so it belongs at the beginning rather than after them.
notes.D: VLDL is less dense than LDL and HDL. Chylomicrons are the least dense, so they belong at the end.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Atherosclerosis is a disease where capillary walls become less elastic and thicker.
Reason: fatty materials accumulate beneath the outer lining of the capillary wall.
questions.why: Atherosclerosis is a disease of the intima of medium and large arteries. Retained apoB-containing lipoproteins and subsequent inflammatory and fibrous responses contribute to plaque formation. The defining process does not take place in capillary walls.

notes.A: Both claims misidentify capillaries as the site of disease. Plaques form in the arterial intima rather than beneath an outer capillary lining.
notes.B: The vessel and layer descriptions are both inaccurate, so neither claim supplies a valid explanation.
notes.C: Plaque-related thickening involves arteries, not capillaries. The assertion therefore misstates the affected vessels.
notes.D: Lipid retention occurs in the arterial intima. The reason is also inaccurate because it places the lesion in capillaries.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Bile salts are not essential to lipid metabolism.
Reason: bile salts can be produced by the body.
questions.why: The assertion is false; bile salts are essential for emulsifying lipids. The reason is true.

notes.A: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.C: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase may not be the most desirable method for controlling cholesterol levels.
Reason: mevalonate is needed for the synthesis of important molecules such as acetyl CoA.
questions.why: The assertion is true. The reason is false: mevalonate is a precursor for cholesterol, CoQ10, and dolichol, but not acetyl CoA.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the reason is false.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is false.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true.

questions.stem: Kofi, a 35-year-old, has been diagnosed with severe hypercholesterolaemia. Which of the following plasma cholesterol levels would indicate this condition?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: A total plasma cholesterol above 7.0 mmol/L is markedly elevated among these choices. Clinical decisions also depend on the LDL cholesterol value, family history and other findings, rather than total cholesterol alone.

notes.B: Low bile acid concentrations can affect intestinal fat handling. They are not a plasma cholesterol measurement.
notes.C: Fat malabsorption can result from several digestive disorders. It does not itself indicate markedly elevated plasma cholesterol.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase participates in cholesterol synthesis. Deficiency of the enzyme is not a measured high cholesterol level.
notes.E: An absence of a heart attack does not exclude high plasma cholesterol. Cholesterol is measured directly.

questions.stem: Which finding would cause impaired emulsification of dietary fat?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Bile salts help stabilise small lipid droplets and form mixed micelles that carry lipid digestion products. Low delivery of bile salts to the intestine can impair emulsification and make fat absorption less efficient.

notes.A: High plasma cholesterol measures a circulating lipid concentration. It does not show that too few bile salts reach the intestinal lumen.
notes.C: Impaired fat absorption can follow defective emulsification. It is a possible result rather than the upstream loss of an emulsifying agent.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is part of cholesterol synthesis, but the most direct defect here is reduced intestinal availability of bile salts.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not explain how dietary fat is dispersed in the intestine.

questions.stem: Low emulsification may lead to one of these clinical presentations:

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Poor emulsification can limit access of lipases to dietary fat and can accompany insufficient mixed-micelle formation. This reduces absorption of long-chain lipid products and can lead to fatty stools and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.

notes.A: Defective emulsification directly affects intestinal lipid processing. A high plasma cholesterol level is not its expected presentation.
notes.B: A low bile salt supply can cause defective emulsification. It is an upstream factor rather than the resulting problem with nutrient uptake.
notes.D: HMG-CoA reductase is involved in cholesterol synthesis. Deficient activity is not a clinical manifestation diagnostic of low emulsification.
notes.E: The absence of a heart attack does not indicate whether dietary fat is being digested and absorbed.

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is contrary to hypercholesterolaemia?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: Hypercholesterolemia directly causes atherosclerosis, which drastically increases the risk of heart attacks. Therefore, stating the patient 'may not suffer a heart attack' is contrary to the disease.

notes.A: This defines hypercholesterolaemia rather than contradicting it.
notes.B: Low bile salts do not contradict high cholesterol.
notes.C: This points to low, not high, cholesterol, but it is a separate problem rather than a presentation contrary to the disease.
notes.D: This is a cause of low cholesterol, not a presentation.

questions.stem: Besides congenital enzyme deficiency, which of these conditions could result in hypocholesterolaemia?

options.label: E
options.text: Patient may not suffer from heart attack

questions.why: If the body cannot absorb dietary fats/cholesterol from the gut, plasma cholesterol levels will drop significantly.

notes.A: This is HYPERcholesterolaemia.
notes.B: Low bile salts reduce fat absorption, but the direct cause asked about is the failure to absorb fat.
notes.D: This IS a congenital enzyme deficiency, which the question excludes.
notes.E: This is not a cause of low cholesterol.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a source of cholesterol?
questions.why: Carrots are plant foods and are not a meaningful dietary source of cholesterol. Plant tissues primarily contain phytosterols. Butter, cheese and egg yolk are animal foods that contribute cholesterol.

notes.A: Butter contains dairy fat and can provide dietary cholesterol, although the amount depends on the serving.
notes.B: Cheese is made from milk and contains some cholesterol, with variation according to fat content and serving size.
notes.C: Egg yolk contains cholesterol in its lipid fraction, in contrast to typical plant foods.

questions.stem: Which of the following is derived from a sterol?
questions.why: Bile salts are derived from cholesterol. Hepatocytes convert the sterol into primary bile acids, which can be conjugated with glycine or taurine before secretion into bile.

notes.B: Gangliosides are glycosphingolipids built from ceramide and an oligosaccharide that contains sialic acid.
notes.C: Geraniol is a monoterpene alcohol formed from isoprenoid precursors. It is not made by modifying a sterol.
notes.D: Phosphatidylglycerol is a glycerophospholipid with a glycerol head group. Its backbone is not cholesterol.
notes.E: Prostaglandins are eicosanoids formed from polyunsaturated fatty acids, often arachidonic acid.

questions.stem: Mechanism of action of statins in the treatment of hypercholesterolaemia:
questions.why: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, slowing conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate. Lower hepatic cholesterol increases LDL receptor expression, which promotes removal of LDL from blood.

notes.B: Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triglycerides in circulating particles. It is not the direct enzyme target of statins.
notes.C: The direct drug effect is inhibition of the reductase, even though feedback can increase expression of the enzyme.
notes.D: Lower plasma LDL reflects increased hepatic clearance through LDL receptors. Direct blockade of LDL particle synthesis is not the main mechanism.
notes.E: Some statins modestly change HDL cholesterol, but inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase is the defining drug action.

questions.stem: Antioxidant is:

options.label: A
options.text: a substance which catalyzes the formation of free radicals

options.label: B
options.text: a substance which neutralizes the formation of free radicals

questions.why: Antioxidants inhibit oxidation by removing reactive species, interrupting radical chain reactions or preventing reactive species from forming. The exact mechanism depends on the particular antioxidant.

notes.A: A substance that promotes radical formation is acting as a pro-oxidant under those conditions.

questions.stem: The antioxidant properties of a substance depends on:

options.label: A
options.text: The molecular structure of the substance

options.label: B
options.text: The redox state of the surrounding environment

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of oxygen and transition metal ions

questions.why: Antioxidant activity depends on a compound's structure and on conditions around it. The local redox state, oxygen availability and transition metals can change which reactions occur and whether the compound has a net antioxidant effect.

notes.A: Molecular structure affects how readily a compound can donate electrons, stabilise a radical or enter a particular cellular compartment.
notes.B: The local redox state can affect whether the compound is available in a form that scavenges reactive species or is regenerated after reacting.
notes.C: Oxygen and transition metals influence radical formation and can change the net effect of a compound in a particular environment.

questions.stem: The free radical causes damage to:
questions.why: Free radicals can damage many classes of cell molecules. They initiate lipid peroxidation, oxidise proteins and carbohydrates, and modify DNA bases or the sugar–phosphate backbone.

notes.A: Radicals can attack polyunsaturated fatty acids and initiate a chain reaction of membrane lipid peroxidation.
notes.B: Oxidative attack can modify carbohydrates, including the deoxyribose backbone in DNA and sugars in other cell structures.
notes.C: Oxidation can modify amino acid side chains and alter the structure, stability or activity of proteins.
notes.D: Reactive species can modify DNA bases and contribute to strand breaks or other lesions.

questions.stem: Dietary carotenoids are efficient quenchers of singlet oxygen:

options.label: A
options.text: Due to their wide distribution in nature

options.label: B
options.text: Due to their highly conjugated double-bond system

options.label: C
options.text: Due to the presence of methyl group in their structure

questions.why: Carotenoids have extended systems of conjugated double bonds. These allow them to accept excitation energy from singlet oxygen and dissipate it, usually as heat, returning oxygen toward its ground state.

notes.A: How widely a pigment occurs in nature does not explain its molecular capacity to quench singlet oxygen.
notes.C: Methyl groups can influence overall structure, but the extended conjugated system is the key feature for efficient energy transfer.
notes.D: The conjugated electron system provides a recognised mechanism for singlet oxygen quenching.

questions.stem: How are anti-oxidants believed to be helpful to our bodies?

options.label: A
options.text: they antagonistically bind to oxygen molecules, thus preventing aerobic pathways

options.label: B
options.text: they enhance free-radical formation, thus increasing the efficiency of cellular processes

options.label: C
options.text: they 'quench' the reactivity of reactive oxygen species, thus preventing their detrimental interactions

options.label: D
options.text: they complex with vitamins in our bodies to produce reactive oxygen species

questions.why: Antioxidant systems limit damage by removing reactive oxygen species or interrupting the reactions they start. This can protect cell components without blocking the ordinary use of oxygen in aerobic metabolism.

notes.A: Antioxidants do not generally block aerobic pathways by binding molecular oxygen. They target specific reactive intermediates or their reactions.
notes.B: Deliberately increasing radical formation is a pro-oxidant effect. It is not the usual protective action of antioxidants.
notes.D: Some vitamins themselves participate in antioxidant systems. Generating reactive oxygen species by complexing with vitamins is not the general mechanism.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? The Fenton reaction:

options.label: A
options.text: results in the formation of hydroxyl radicals

options.label: B
options.text: involves redox cycling of Fe(III) to Fe(II) and vice versa

options.label: C
options.text: results in electrons being transferred from superoxide anions to hydrogen peroxide

questions.why: The Fenton reaction generates highly toxic hydroxyl radicals; it does not protect against oxidative stress.

notes.A: True: Fe2+ + H2O2 gives OH•.
notes.B: True: iron cycles between Fe3+ and Fe2+.
notes.C: True: superoxide reduces Fe3+, which then reacts with H2O2 (the Haber–Weiss reaction).

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? The superoxide anion is:

options.label: B
options.text: a free radical reactive oxygen species

options.label: C
options.text: converted to water by superoxide dismutase

options.label: D
options.text: able to react with hydrogen peroxide producing hydroxyl radicals

questions.why: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen. Catalase and peroxidases then remove hydrogen peroxide, so water is not the direct product of superoxide dismutase.

notes.A: Mitochondrial electron transfer can reduce oxygen one electron at a time and produce superoxide.
notes.B: Superoxide has an unpaired electron and is classified as a radical reactive oxygen species.
notes.D: Superoxide can participate in metal-catalysed production of hydroxyl radical from hydrogen peroxide. The direct uncatalysed reaction is very slow.

questions.stem: It is untrue that with respect to reactive oxygen species:

options.label: A
options.text: the superoxide anion is a free radical

options.label: B
options.text: hydrogen peroxide is a free radical

options.label: C
options.text: the hydroxyl radical is extremely reactive

questions.why: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but not a free radical, because it has no unpaired electron. Superoxide is a radical, the hydroxyl radical is the most reactive species known in biology, and H2O2 crosses membranes because it is lipid soluble.

notes.A: True: superoxide has an unpaired electron.
notes.C: True: OH• is the most reactive ROS.
notes.D: True: H2O2 is uncharged and diffuses across membranes.

questions.stem: A young boy has fever for which Antimalarial drugs have been administered. Following this he passed black coloured Urine, which improved after four days. Which condition should be considered as a Likely possibility?
questions.why: Red cells use G6PD to generate NADPH and maintain reduced glutathione. Certain oxidant antimalarials can trigger haemolysis in people with G6PD deficiency, causing dark urine from free haemoglobin. Malaria itself can also cause haemolysis.

notes.A: Acute nephritis can cause dark urine from red cells in the urine. The timing after an oxidant exposure raises concern for haemolysis in this vignette.
notes.C: Hepatitis can darken urine through conjugated bilirubin, but that differs mechanistically from the possible haemoglobinuria after oxidative red-cell injury.
notes.D: Haematuria means intact red cells are present in urine. Intravascular haemolysis can instead release free haemoglobin into urine.

questions.stem: What enzyme, or combination of enzymes, protects cells against superoxide generated in oxidation reactions?
questions.why: SOD converts superoxide to H2O2, and catalase then converts the H2O2 into water and oxygen.

notes.A: SOD alone leaves H2O2, which is still harmful.
notes.B: Catalase cannot act on superoxide.
notes.D: Glutathione peroxidase removes peroxides, not superoxide.

questions.stem: All of the following enzymes may contribute in generating free oxygen radicals within neutrophils for killing intracellular bacteria except?
questions.why: Glutathione peroxidase detoxifies peroxides; it does not generate radicals.

notes.A: SOD in the phagosome makes H2O2, which feeds radical generation.
notes.B: The Fenton reaction makes OH• (it is a reaction, not an enzyme).
notes.C: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide (the respiratory burst).

questions.stem: The glutathione cycle is the conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione in the presence of NADPH. Which of the following enzyme catalyzes this reaction?
questions.why: Glutathione reductase uses NADPH to reduce the disulphide bond of oxidised glutathione. This regenerates two reduced glutathione molecules for use in antioxidant reactions.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove peroxides, forming oxidised glutathione in the process.
notes.B: The standard enzyme that regenerates reduced glutathione from its disulphide is glutathione reductase. This reaction uses NADPH.
notes.D: Glutathione synthetase forms glutathione by adding glycine during biosynthesis. It does not reduce oxidised glutathione.

questions.stem: Free radicals can be inactivated by the following enzymes EXCEPT:
questions.why: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to produce hypochlorous acid in phagocytes. Its characteristic role is to generate a reactive antimicrobial oxidant, unlike antioxidant systems that remove superoxide or peroxides.

notes.A: Glutathione peroxidase uses reduced glutathione to remove hydrogen peroxide or lipid hydroperoxides.
notes.B: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, limiting peroxide accumulation.
notes.C: Superoxide dismutase converts the superoxide radical to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen so other enzymes can handle the peroxide.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is not true with respect to detoxification of ROS?

options.label: A
options.text: superoxide dismutase (SOD) is found in both mitochondria and cytoplasm

options.label: B
options.text: SOD catalyzes the conversion of superoxide anions to hydrogen peroxide

options.label: C
options.text: catalase converts hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen

options.label: D
options.text: glutathione catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen peroxide to water

questions.why: Glutathione is a reducing substrate rather than the catalyst. Glutathione peroxidase catalyses peroxide reduction using reduced glutathione, which is oxidised in the process.

notes.A: Different superoxide dismutase forms occur in the cytosol and mitochondria, protecting those cellular compartments.
notes.B: Dismutation of superoxide produces hydrogen peroxide and molecular oxygen.
notes.C: Catalase removes hydrogen peroxide through a reaction that produces water and molecular oxygen.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is not true with respect to oxidative stress?

options.label: B
options.text: mitochondria constantly release hydrogen peroxide into the cytoplasm of cells

options.label: C
options.text: cells possess redox sensors such as KEAP1/Nrf2

options.label: D
options.text: DNA is resistant to oxidative damage

questions.why: DNA can be damaged by reactive oxygen species. Oxidation can generate modified bases such as 8-oxoguanine and contribute to strand breaks, so antioxidant defences and DNA repair are important.

notes.A: Healthy cells have systems that balance the production and removal of reactive species and maintain a suitable redox environment.
notes.B: Mitochondrial metabolism can generate hydrogen peroxide, some of which can reach the cytosol and participate in redox signalling.
notes.C: The KEAP1–NRF2 system senses changes in oxidative and electrophilic stress and regulates expression of protective genes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most reactive free radical in the body?
questions.why: The hydroxyl radical reacts extremely rapidly with many nearby molecules, including lipids, proteins and DNA. It often causes damage near the site where it forms because its lifetime is so short.

notes.B: Superoxide is a radical that participates in redox reactions, but it is generally less reactive toward many targets than hydroxyl radical.
notes.C: Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive oxygen species but not a free radical because it has no unpaired electron.
notes.D: Organic oxygen-centred radicals can participate in oxidative reactions. Hydroxyl radical is usually the most rapidly reacting species among these choices.

questions.stem: True or false: Different anti-oxidants are needed to protect oxidative stress and cell injury.
questions.why: Different antioxidants protect different compartments or act at different stages of oxidation. Some remove peroxides, while others interrupt lipid radical chains or regenerate the active form of another antioxidant.

notes.B: A single antioxidant does not protect equally against all oxidants or in every cellular compartment.

questions.stem: True or false: Failure to find lipid peroxidation does not rule out the occurrence of oxidative stress.
questions.why: Oxidative stress can damage proteins, nucleic acids or other targets without producing detectable lipid peroxidation. The absence of one marker therefore does not rule out redox imbalance.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation is only one potential result of oxidative stress. Other targets can be damaged even when this marker is absent.

questions.stem: True or false: A chain-breaking antioxidant such as Vit. E is a therapeutic event.
questions.why: Chain-breaking antioxidants stop the propagation of lipid peroxidation.

questions.stem: True or false: Oncogenesis can occur during lipid peroxidation.
questions.why: Lipid peroxidation can produce reactive aldehydes that form DNA adducts or alter signalling. These effects can contribute to mutations or processes associated with tumour development, although peroxidation alone does not determine whether cancer occurs.

notes.B: Lipid peroxidation can have effects beyond the membrane. Its reactive products can modify DNA and participate in processes that contribute to oncogenesis.

questions.stem: True or false: Ascorbic acid, zinc and Selenium are recommended supplementary antioxidant therapies.
questions.why: Vitamin C is a direct antioxidant; Zinc and Selenium are essential cofactors for antioxidant enzymes.

questions.stem: True or false: DNA damage can result in the generation of reactive oxidative species.
questions.why: DNA injury can activate cellular stress pathways that change mitochondrial or enzyme activity and lead to additional reactive oxygen species. Oxidative species can also cause DNA damage, so the association can operate in both directions.

notes.B: DNA damage is not only an outcome of oxidative stress. A damage response can also increase oxidant generation in some settings.

questions.stem:
In the light of Reactive Oxidative Species (ROS):
I. ROS are generated as a consequence to the body's own natural processes.
II. Disease processes can generate reactive radicals in presence of hydrogen peroxide.
III. ROS can be generated consequent to tissue damage.
questions.why: Reactive oxygen species can arise during normal metabolism, including mitochondrial electron transfer. Disease and tissue injury can increase their formation through inflammatory or metal-catalysed reactions, including reactions involving hydrogen peroxide.

notes.A: Normal metabolism is a source, but disease and tissue injury can also change oxidant production.
notes.B: Endogenous metabolism and peroxide-related reactions are relevant, and damaged tissue can also contribute to reactive species formation.
notes.C: A focus on disease and damage omits the low-level oxidant production that occurs in normal cellular metabolism.
notes.D: Normal metabolism and injured tissue are sources. Hydrogen peroxide can also give rise to more reactive species through metal-catalysed reactions.

questions.stem:
Considering the eukaryotic cell, any of these cellular organelles can be a source of ROS:
I. Nucleus
II. Mitochondria
III. Cytoplasm
questions.why: Reactive oxygen species can originate in several cellular compartments. Mitochondrial electron transfer is a common source, while oxidant-generating enzymes and redox reactions can contribute in the cytoplasm and nuclear region.

notes.A: The nucleus can experience local generation of oxidants, but mitochondria and cytosolic reactions can also contribute.
notes.B: Mitochondria are a major source, but reactive oxygen species are not generated exclusively in mitochondria.
notes.C: Nuclear and mitochondrial sources are possible. Cytoplasmic enzyme reactions can also contribute to oxidant formation.
notes.D: Cytoplasmic and mitochondrial sources are well recognised. Redox-active processes in the nuclear region can also generate reactive species.

questions.stem:
The following are rich sources of anti-oxidants:
I. coffee
II. almond nuts
III. mushrooms
questions.why: Coffee contains phenolic compounds, almonds provide vitamin E, and many mushrooms contain compounds such as ergothioneine. Each can supply substances with antioxidant properties, although amounts and biological effects differ.

notes.A: Coffee contributes compounds such as chlorogenic acids. Almonds and mushrooms also contain compounds with antioxidant properties.
notes.B: Coffee and almonds both contribute antioxidant compounds, and some mushrooms are a dietary source of ergothioneine.
notes.C: Almonds and mushrooms supply antioxidant compounds. Coffee also contains phenolic substances rather than supplying caffeine alone.
notes.D: Coffee and mushrooms contribute antioxidant compounds. Almonds are also a source of vitamin E and other dietary antioxidants.

questions.stem:
The following are generally extracellular anti-oxidant defences:
I. Lactoferrin
II. Ceruloplasmin
III. Haptoglobin
questions.why: Extracellular proteins can limit oxidation by keeping redox-active metals or haem away from vulnerable molecules. Lactoferrin binds iron, ceruloplasmin oxidises ferrous iron for safe transport, and haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin.

notes.A: Lactoferrin limits the availability of free iron. Ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin also help limit metal- or haem-associated oxidation.
notes.B: Ceruloplasmin has ferroxidase activity that supports iron handling, but it is one of several extracellular protective proteins.
notes.C: Sequestering iron and supporting safer iron transport are protective. Haptoglobin adds a separate defence by binding free haemoglobin.
notes.D: Ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin limit oxidative injury in different ways. Lactoferrin adds protection by binding iron.

questions.stem:
The following anti-oxidants remove free radicals by directly reacting with them catalytically:
I. GSH
II. Vit. C
III. Urate
questions.why: Glutathione and Vitamin C can act catalytically (they are regenerated). Urate acts stoichiometrically.

notes.A: Leaves out II, which is also true.
notes.C: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes III, which is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following is likely to be associated with lipid peroxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: Intermittent generation of OH* can combine with O2 to give only alkoxyl radicals

options.label: B
options.text: Hydroxyl radicals during lipid peroxidation can generate peroxyl moieties to give rise to alkoxyl radicals

options.label: C
options.text: Free radicals reactions during lipid peroxidation can combine with nearby saturated fatty acids

options.label: D
options.text: Hydroxyl radicals during lipid peroxidation can combine with O2 to give peroxyl radicals capable of abstracting H* and forming peroxides

questions.why: The mechanism is: OH* attacks a polyunsaturated fatty acid to form a lipid radical. This radical reacts with O2 to form a lipid peroxyl radical.

notes.A: Peroxyl radicals form, not only alkoxyl radicals.
notes.B: The order is reversed: peroxyl radicals come from lipid radicals plus O2.
notes.C: Polyunsaturated fatty acids are attacked, not saturated ones.

questions.stem: True or false: Protein degradation consequent to free radical attack occurs at the molecular level.
questions.why: Oxidative attack can modify amino acid side chains, cleave a protein backbone or cause cross-linking. These molecular changes can impair function and make damaged proteins more susceptible to cellular degradation.

notes.B: Radical injury can change the protein molecule itself and can promote degradation of the damaged protein.

questions.stem:
Which of the following antioxidants are generated internally?
I. GSH
II. Urate
III. Vitamin C
questions.why: Human cells synthesise glutathione from amino acids, and urate is generated during purine breakdown. Humans lack a functional final enzyme for vitamin C synthesis and must obtain it from the diet.

notes.A: Glutathione is produced internally, but human purine catabolism also produces urate.
notes.C: Urate is formed in the body, whereas vitamin C must normally come from food. This pair also omits glutathione.
notes.D: Both glutathione and urate are made internally. Vitamin C is excluded because humans cannot complete its biosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true? Paraquat is:

options.label: C
options.text: able to receive electrons from superoxide anions

options.label: D
options.text: cytotoxic to type I and II pneumocytes

options.label: E
options.text: catalyzes the flow of electrons from NADPH/NADH to oxygen

questions.why: In the usual model of paraquat toxicity, cellular reductases transfer electrons to paraquat using reduced cofactors. Reduced paraquat then transfers an electron to molecular oxygen, generating superoxide, rather than using superoxide as its normal electron donor.

notes.A: Paraquat participates in repeated reduction and oxidation, which is the basis of its redox activity.
notes.B: Ingestion can result in systemic absorption, although only a portion of the dose is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract.
notes.D: Lung cells, including pneumocytes, can be injured by reactive species generated during paraquat redox cycling.
notes.E: The cycle transfers reducing equivalents from cellular cofactors to oxygen, resulting in the formation of superoxide.

questions.stem: Free radicals are capable of independent existence and have a single unpaired electron. Which of the following best describes a reactive oxygen species (ROS)?

options.label: A
options.text: Free radicals capable of interacting with oxygen

options.label: B
options.text: Free radicals that cannot interact with oxygen

options.label: C
options.text: Oxygen compounds that are reactive free radicals

options.label: D
options.text: Oxygen compounds that can only react with free radicals

options.label: E
options.text: Oxygen compounds that cannot react with free radicals

questions.why: ROS includes oxygen compounds that are reactive free radicals (and non-radical derivatives like H2O2).

notes.A: Too vague: an ROS is itself an oxygen species.
notes.B: ROS are oxygen-derived.
notes.D: ROS react with many molecules, not only with free radicals.
notes.E: ROS do react with free radicals.

questions.stem:
The following are Eukaryotic cellular sources of Free radicals;
I. Lysosomes
II. Cell membranes
III. Mitochondria
questions.why: Free radicals can originate in several cellular compartments. Mitochondrial electron transfer can generate superoxide, membrane-associated oxidases can generate reactive species, and reactions involving redox-active metals in lysosomes can form radicals.

notes.B: Lysosomes and membrane-associated reactions can generate radicals, but mitochondrial electron transfer is also a major source.
notes.C: Cell membranes and mitochondria are important sites. Iron-dependent reactions in lysosomes can also contribute.
notes.D: Lysosomal chemistry can generate radicals under some conditions, but radicals can also originate at membranes and inside mitochondria.
notes.E: The cell contains multiple sites capable of generating radicals, including mitochondria and some membrane-bound enzyme systems.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements; select the correct one(s):
I. Oxidative protein damage occurs during X-ray crystallography.
II. Oxidative protein damage consequent to a free radical attack can impair the functioning of receptors.
III. Oxidative protein damage consequent to a free radical attack cannot impair the activities of antibodies.
questions.why: X-ray exposure can damage proteins during crystallography, in part through radiolysis and reactive species. Oxidation can also alter cellular receptors or antibodies, so antibodies are not inherently protected from oxidative impairment.

notes.A: The claim that antibody activity cannot be altered is too strong. Oxidation can change antigen binding or other antibody properties.
notes.C: Oxidative injury can impair receptors, but antibodies can also be affected. This grouping incorrectly excludes radiation-related protein damage.
notes.D: X-ray damage to a protein is possible, and radical attack can also impair normal receptor function.
notes.E: Radiation-induced protein damage and functional impairment of oxidised receptors are both recognised processes.

questions.stem:
The following are rich sources of anti-oxidants:
I. coffee
II. almond nuts
III. mushrooms
questions.why: Coffee can supply phenolic compounds, almonds are a source of vitamin E, and mushrooms can contain ergothioneine. All three can contribute dietary compounds with antioxidant properties, with amounts varying by food and preparation.

notes.B: Coffee and almonds provide antioxidant compounds. Mushrooms can also contribute compounds such as ergothioneine.
notes.C: Almonds and mushrooms are examples, but coffee also contains compounds such as chlorogenic acids.
notes.D: Coffee is a source of phenolics. Almonds provide vitamin E, and mushrooms can also contain antioxidant compounds.
notes.E: Each of the three foods contains compounds with antioxidant properties, although that does not establish clinical benefit from a given serving.

questions.stem:
The following are generally intracellular anti-oxidant defences:
I. Urate
II. Alpha-tocopherol
III. Transferrin
questions.why: Alpha-tocopherol is a lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant that protects cell membrane lipids from peroxidation. In this comparison, circulating urate and transferrin are classically discussed as extracellular defences. Alpha-tocopherol is also transported in plasma lipoproteins.

notes.A: Plasma urate scavenges some oxidants and transferrin binds iron, so the complete group is not usually classified as intracellular.
notes.B: Urate is a prominent antioxidant in extracellular fluid, while alpha-tocopherol protects the lipid compartment of cell membranes.
notes.D: Urate contributes strongly to circulating antioxidant capacity. The membrane-localised antioxidant among these choices is alpha-tocopherol.
notes.E: Alpha-tocopherol can act in a cellular compartment by interrupting oxidation chains within membranes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is associated with lipid peroxidation?

options.label: A
options.text: Initial OH attack can generate free radicals to combine with O2 to give only alkoxyl radicals.

options.label: B
options.text: Initial OH attack can generate peroxyls moieties to give alkoxyl radicals.

questions.why: A hydroxyl radical can start lipid peroxidation by abstracting hydrogen from a lipid. The lipid radical reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical. Breakdown of subsequent lipid hydroperoxides can generate alkoxyl radicals.

notes.A: A lipid radical reacts with oxygen initially to form a lipid peroxyl radical. Alkoxyl radicals may form later when hydroperoxides decompose.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Antioxidants like selenium are crucial to the body antioxidant defense system.
Reason: Antioxidants like selenium have reversible oxidative states.
questions.why: Both are true. However, selenium works by being incorporated into enzymes (like glutathione peroxidase), not just by its own reversible oxidation.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason does not explain the assertion.
notes.C: Wrong here: the reason is true.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Foods like carrot, oranges, Water melon are rich in vitamins and antioxidants.
Reason: they are fruits.
questions.why: Carrots, oranges and watermelon contain nutrients such as carotenoids or vitamin C. Botanically, a carrot is a storage root, whereas oranges and watermelons are fruits. Their chemistry, rather than a single food classification, accounts for their nutrient content.

notes.A: The nutrient assertion is reasonable, but the classification of all three as fruits is incorrect.
notes.B: The reason is not true for carrots, which are edible storage roots.
notes.D: The assertion is supported by their nutrient content, while the reason misclassifies carrots as fruit.
notes.E: The fruit classification is inaccurate, but these foods do contain vitamins and compounds with antioxidant properties.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Free radicals, which are harmful to the body, can form from events such as aging.
Reason: Free radicals are also by products of the body's natural processes.
questions.why: Both true. Aging is associated with free radical formation, which are generated as byproducts of normal metabolism.

notes.B: Wrong here: the reason does explain the assertion.
notes.C: Wrong here: the reason is true.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is true.

questions.stem: PARKINSON's Disease (Oxidative Stress Context)

notes.A: Increased lipid oxidation products have been reported in Parkinson disease, consistent with oxidative injury to membranes.
notes.B: Mitochondrial dysfunction, dopamine metabolism and other factors can contribute to oxidative stress in affected tissue.
notes.C: A consistent decrease in oxidised glutathione is not established. Nigral studies have often highlighted depletion of the reduced form.
notes.D: Reduced glutathione is often decreased in the substantia nigra. An increase is not the characteristic observation.

questions.why: Oxidative stress is associated with Parkinson disease, including lipid oxidation and depletion of reduced glutathione in the substantia nigra. Changes in oxidised glutathione are less consistent and depend on the tissue and measurement.

questions.stem: ROS Activity at Cellular Levels

options.label: A
options.text: Free radicals are the major cause of Aging and declined health

options.label: B
options.text: The body employs antioxidants to handle free radicals

options.label: C
options.text: Excessive free radicals production and the resulting oxidative stress can harm cell components

options.label: D
options.text: Aging process becomes rapid and also increases the risk of degenerative diseases

notes.A: This is the free radical theory of ageing, accepted at this level.
notes.B: Enzymes and dietary antioxidants neutralise free radicals.
notes.C: Lipids, proteins and DNA are all damaged.
notes.D: Accumulated oxidative damage speeds ageing and raises the risk of degenerative disease.

questions.why: The free-radical theory holds that ROS, when they exceed antioxidant defences, damage lipids, proteins and DNA, speeding ageing and degenerative disease.

questions.stem: y-glutamylcysteine is a precursor to glutathione. Glutathione synthesized helps prevent:
questions.why: Gamma-glutamylcysteine is combined with glycine to form glutathione. Reduced glutathione supplies reducing equivalents to peroxidases, helping remove hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides before they cause oxidative damage.

notes.B: Glutathione helps maintain the cell's redox environment by reducing oxidants. The protection described is against oxidative damage.

questions.stem: When Free Radicals surmounts the counteract effect of antioxidants; it results to:
