questions.why: Oxidative stress is a disturbance in redox control in which oxidant generation exceeds the ability of antioxidant systems to handle it. The resulting reactions can damage lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.

notes.B: Toxicity is a broad term for harmful effects. Oxidative stress specifically describes the imbalance between oxidants and antioxidant capacity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a source of free radicals:
questions.why: Cytochrome P450 reactions can leak electrons, activated phagocytes can make superoxide, and alloxan can undergo redox cycling. Lipid peroxidation also propagates radical intermediates, so each of the listed processes can contribute to free radicals.

notes.A: Uncoupled cytochrome P450 activity can release reactive species during electron transfer to oxygen.
notes.B: Activated phagocytes produce superoxide through an NADPH oxidase-dependent respiratory burst.
notes.C: Alloxan can generate reactive species through redox cycling and contribute to oxidative injury.
notes.D: Lipid peroxidation is a chain reaction in which lipid and lipid peroxyl radicals are formed.

questions.stem: What amino acids are found in protein?
questions.why: Ribosomes incorporate mainly L-alpha amino acids, with glycine as an achiral exception. Alpha means the amino group is on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group.

notes.A: The usual amino acids in ribosomally synthesised proteins have their amino group at the alpha carbon, rather than the beta carbon.
notes.B: D-beta amino acids differ in both configuration and amino group position from the usual building blocks of proteins.
notes.D: D-alpha amino acids can occur in some biological molecules, but ordinary ribosomal protein synthesis predominantly incorporates the L forms.
notes.E: The structural and stereochemical requirements distinguish the usual protein building blocks from the other amino acid classes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an acidic/basic amino acid?
questions.why: Serine has an uncharged, polar hydroxyl-containing side chain at physiological pH. Lysine and arginine have basic side chains, while glutamate has an acidic carboxylate side chain.

notes.A: The guanidinium side chain of arginine is positively charged at physiological pH and is classified as basic.
notes.B: Lysine has an additional amino group in its side chain. It tends to be protonated and positively charged at physiological pH.
notes.D: Glutamate has a second carboxyl group in its side chain, which is usually negatively charged at physiological pH.

questions.stem: What form of bond holds the amino acid sequence of proteins?
questions.why: The primary sequence is held together by peptide bonds. These covalent amide bonds join the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the amino nitrogen of the next.

notes.A: Disulphide bonds can link two cysteine side chains and stabilise folded structure. They do not join every successive amino acid.
notes.C: Peptide bonds are covalent. The more specific name for the bond linking adjacent residues in a protein backbone is a peptide bond.
notes.D: Hydrogen bonding stabilises folding patterns such as alpha helices and beta sheets. It does not make the primary backbone linkage.

questions.stem: The secondary structure of amino Acids peptides are held by which form of bond?
questions.why: Alpha helices and beta sheets are stabilised largely by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens. The arrangements differ in where the participating peptide groups lie along the chain.

notes.A: Disulphide bridges join cysteine side chains and often support higher levels of folding. They do not form the common backbone pattern of secondary structure.
notes.B: Peptide bonds join amino acids to make the primary backbone. Hydrogen bonds between peptide groups stabilise recurring secondary structures.
notes.D: Covalent bonds make up the chain itself. Alpha helices and beta sheets are distinguished by the pattern of backbone hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not involved in cystinuria?
questions.why: Cystinuria impairs tubular reabsorption of cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, ornithine and arginine. Tryptophan is a neutral aromatic amino acid and does not use this affected transport system.

notes.A: Poorly soluble cystine can accumulate in urine and form stones when its tubular reabsorption is impaired.
notes.B: Lysine is a dibasic amino acid normally transported by the affected system and can be increased in urine.
notes.C: Ornithine is one of the dibasic substrates whose proximal tubular uptake is defective in cystinuria.

questions.stem: The Nitrogen in urea Cycle is derived from;
questions.why: The two nitrogen atoms in urea come from different sources. One enters as free ammonia, incorporated into carbamoyl phosphate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. The other is donated by aspartate during argininosuccinate formation.

notes.A: Ornithine accepts the carbamoyl group but is regenerated by arginase. It does not supply the second nitrogen of urea.
notes.B: Aspartate donates one nitrogen, but ornithine cycles through the pathway. The other nitrogen arrives via carbamoyl phosphate.
notes.C: Glutamate can supply ammonia or amino groups upstream. The immediate nitrogen donors are carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate.
notes.E: Carbamoyl phosphate supplies one nitrogen. Aspartate, rather than glutamate directly, supplies the second.

questions.stem: What is the role of N-acetyl glutamate in ureogenesis?
questions.why: N-acetylglutamate is the obligatory allosteric activator of mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. It increases the liver's ability to incorporate ammonia nitrogen into the urea cycle.

notes.B: AMP is a nucleotide, rather than the enzyme activated by N-acetylglutamate in ureogenesis.
notes.C: Ornithine transcarbamylase uses carbamoyl phosphate in the next reaction. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is the direct target of N-acetylglutamate.

questions.stem: The major regulatory step in urea cycle is catalyzed by;
questions.why: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I catalyses the first committed reaction of ureogenesis in liver mitochondria. It uses ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP, and its activity depends on the allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate.

notes.B: Ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine after carbamoyl phosphate has been made.
notes.C: Argininosuccinate synthetase uses aspartate to supply the second nitrogen in the cytosolic portion of the cycle.
notes.D: Argininosuccinate lyase forms arginine and fumarate downstream of the major regulatory reaction.
notes.E: Arginase releases urea in the final reaction and regenerates ornithine. It is not the principal entry-point regulator.

questions.stem: Ammonia generated in the body enters the urea cycle in which of the following forms?
questions.why: The two nitrogen atoms of urea enter through the mitochondrial ammonia–ammonium pool and through the amino group of aspartate. The first is incorporated into carbamoyl phosphate, and aspartate donates the other nitrogen during argininosuccinate synthesis.

notes.A: Glutamine can carry nitrogen to the liver and release it as ammonia. It is not the immediate amino-group donor in argininosuccinate synthesis.
notes.C: Glutamate can supply nitrogen through deamination or transamination, but aspartate is the second direct donor to the cycle.
notes.D: Glutamate is an important upstream nitrogen source. The two immediate inputs are the ammonia–ammonium pool and aspartate.

questions.stem: The glucose alanine cycle puts burden on the liver via gluconeogenesis. Which of the following acts as the acceptor of the amino group in the liver?
questions.why: Hepatic alanine aminotransferase transfers alanine's amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and pyruvate. The liver can use the pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and dispose of the transferred nitrogen through the urea cycle.

notes.A: Glutamate is the product formed when alpha-ketoglutarate accepts the amino group from alanine.
notes.B: Glutamine can carry nitrogen between tissues, but it is not the keto acid that accepts nitrogen in the hepatic alanine aminotransferase reaction.
notes.D: Aspartate is an important nitrogen donor in the urea cycle. It is not the immediate acceptor used by alanine aminotransferase in this reaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following amino acid: Keto acid pair bridges the urea cycle with the tricarboxylic acid cycle for the maintenance of the nitrogen and amino acid pool?
questions.why: Aspartate aminotransferase interconverts aspartate and oxaloacetate. Fumarate produced in the urea cycle can feed into malate and oxaloacetate, which can regenerate the aspartate required by the cycle.

notes.A: Glutamate and alpha-ketoglutarate also participate in nitrogen transfer, but the fumarate-to-aspartate link specifically uses oxaloacetate.
notes.C: Alanine and pyruvate are central to the glucose–alanine cycle between muscle and liver. They are not the pair used in the fumarate–aspartate link.
notes.D: The aspartate–oxaloacetate pair provides a direct way to connect urea cycle nitrogen donation with TCA-linked carbon intermediates.

questions.stem: Urea cycle provides intermediate for which pathway?
questions.why: Argininosuccinate lyase produces fumarate during the urea cycle. Fumarate is a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate and can be converted to malate and oxaloacetate, linking the pathways.

notes.A: The urea cycle does not directly supply a standard glycolytic intermediate. Its direct carbon link in this comparison is fumarate.
notes.B: The hexose monophosphate shunt uses sugar phosphates, starting with glucose 6-phosphate. Fumarate is not an intermediate of that pathway.
notes.D: Fumarate-derived carbon can eventually support glucose synthesis, but fumarate itself is directly recognised as a TCA cycle intermediate.

questions.stem: Urea is formed from:
questions.why: Arginase hydrolyses arginine to urea and ornithine. Ornithine then re-enters mitochondria to take part in another turn of the urea cycle.

notes.A: Citrulline is an earlier intermediate that combines with aspartate to make argininosuccinate.
notes.B: Argininosuccinate is split into arginine and fumarate. The arginine produced is the immediate substrate for urea release.
notes.D: Ornithine is the other product of the arginase reaction and is recycled, rather than being hydrolysed to release urea.

questions.stem: An essential amino acid in man is:
questions.why: Methionine is an essential amino acid because humans cannot synthesise enough to meet normal requirements. It must be obtained from the diet and can supply methyl groups through S-adenosylmethionine.

notes.A: Aspartate can be produced by transamination of oxaloacetate and therefore is not an essential dietary amino acid in ordinary conditions.
notes.B: Tyrosine can be made from the essential amino acid phenylalanine when phenylalanine hydroxylase functions normally.
notes.D: Serine can be synthesised from a glycolytic intermediate through a pathway beginning with 3-phosphoglycerate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is semi essential amino acid for humans?
questions.why: Arginine is conditionally essential. Endogenous synthesis can meet the needs of many healthy adults, but dietary supply can become important in growth or other circumstances when requirements exceed production.

notes.A: Valine is a branched-chain essential amino acid that normally has to be supplied in the diet.
notes.C: Lysine is an essential amino acid rather than one ordinarily synthesised in sufficient amounts by humans.
notes.D: Threonine is an essential amino acid and is normally obtained from dietary protein.

questions.stem: An example of polar amino acid is:
questions.why: Arginine is a highly polar, positively charged (basic) amino acid.

notes.A: Alanine is nonpolar.
notes.B: Leucine is nonpolar.
notes.D: Tyrosine is only weakly polar (aromatic); arginine is clearly polar and charged.

questions.stem: The amino acid with a nonpolar side chain is:
questions.why: Valine has a branched hydrocarbon side chain, so it is hydrophobic and nonpolar. The other listed side chains contain hydroxyl or amide groups that can interact with water.

notes.A: Serine has a hydroxyl group in its side chain, making it polar and able to form hydrogen bonds.
notes.C: Asparagine has an uncharged amide side chain that can hydrogen-bond with water or neighbouring groups.
notes.D: Threonine contains a hydroxyl group. Despite its methyl group, it is usually classified as polar uncharged.

questions.stem: A ketogenic amino acid is:
questions.why: Isoleucine is both ketogenic and glucogenic. Its breakdown yields acetyl-CoA, which can contribute to ketone formation, and propionyl-CoA, which can contribute to glucose production through succinyl-CoA.

notes.A: Valine is glucogenic because its carbon is channelled toward succinyl-CoA, rather than yielding a ketogenic product.
notes.B: Cysteine can be degraded to pyruvate, so it is classified as glucogenic in the standard nutritional scheme.
notes.D: Glycine can contribute to gluconeogenesis, for example after conversion to serine. It is not the ketogenic amino acid in this list.

questions.stem: All the following are sulphur containing amino acids found in proteins except:
questions.why: Threonine has an oxygen-containing hydroxyl group and no sulphur in its side chain. Cysteine and methionine contain sulphur. Cystine is an oxidised pair of cysteine residues joined by a disulphide bond.

notes.A: Cysteine contains a thiol group, which can form disulphide bonds with another cysteine residue.
notes.B: Cystine contains two sulphur atoms in its disulphide linkage and can occur within folded proteins.
notes.C: Methionine has a sulphur atom in its thioether side chain.

questions.stem: An aromatic amino acid is:
questions.why: Tyrosine contains a phenolic aromatic ring. This places it with aromatic amino acids, while the hydroxyl group also confers polarity and can participate in hydrogen bonding.

notes.A: Lysine has an aliphatic chain ending in a basic amino group. It does not contain an aromatic ring.
notes.C: Taurine is an amino sulfonic acid without an aromatic ring and is not a standard residue in proteins.
notes.D: Arginine has a basic guanidinium side chain rather than an aromatic ring.

questions.stem: The principal end product of protein metabolism, which is excreted in the greatest quantity in human urine, is:
questions.why: Most nitrogen released from amino acid breakdown is converted by the liver into urea. Urea is water soluble and is excreted by the kidneys, making it the main nitrogenous product of protein metabolism in urine.

notes.B: Glutamine transports nitrogen safely between tissues and can support renal ammonium production. It is not the major form excreted.
notes.C: Ammonium excretion is important in acid–base regulation. Urea normally accounts for a larger share of urinary nitrogen.
notes.D: Uric acid mainly comes from purine breakdown rather than being the major product of amino acid nitrogen disposal.

questions.stem: Glutamate decarboxylation results in formation of inhibitory transmitter in CNS. Name it.
questions.why: Glutamate decarboxylase removes carbon dioxide from glutamate to form gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA. The enzyme uses pyridoxal phosphate, and GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system.

notes.B: Glutathione is a tripeptide formed by joining glutamate, cysteine and glycine. It is not the decarboxylation product of glutamate.
notes.C: Histamine is made by decarboxylation of histidine rather than glutamate.
notes.D: Serotonin is synthesised from tryptophan through hydroxylation followed by decarboxylation.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Transdeamination is a multi-step reaction to generate ammonia.
Reason: Transdeamination involves decarboxylation reaction followed by oxidative deamination.
questions.why: Transdeamination couples transamination to oxidative deamination. Amino groups are first transferred to alpha-ketoglutarate to make glutamate, and glutamate dehydrogenase can then release the nitrogen as ammonia.

notes.A: The assertion is correct, but the reason names decarboxylation instead of the initial transamination step.
notes.B: The first step is amino-group transfer, not loss of carbon dioxide. The reason is therefore not a true description of the sequence.
notes.D: Transdeamination does generate ammonia, so the assertion is true even though the reason states the wrong first step.
notes.E: The reason is inaccurate, but the assertion correctly identifies a route for generating ammonia through more than one reaction.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Alanine-glucose cycle imposes the burden of gluconeogenesis on the liver.
Reason: Alanine-glucose cycle transports alanine from the muscle through the blood to the liver.
questions.why: Both true. The transport of alanine is the mechanism, not the reason why it's a burden.

notes.A: Wrong here: the reason does not explain the assertion.
notes.C: Wrong here: the reason is true.
notes.D: Wrong here: the assertion is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the assertion is true and the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Ureogenesis is an energy expensive process.
Reason: Ureogenesis utilizes two molecules of ATP.
questions.why: The urea cycle consumes three ATP molecules per urea, equivalent to four high-energy phosphate bonds. Two ATP are used to make carbamoyl phosphate and another is converted to AMP during argininosuccinate synthesis.

notes.A: Ureogenesis is energy demanding, but the reason omits the ATP used during argininosuccinate synthesis.
notes.B: Both statements cannot be accepted because the whole cycle consumes more than the two ATP used at its entry step.
notes.D: The assertion is true. The stated cost is incomplete because a further ATP is cleaved to AMP.
notes.E: Three ATP molecules are consumed overall, so the reason is inaccurate but the assertion about energy cost is correct.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Urea cycle predominantly occurs in the mitochondria.
Reason: Urea cycle has four of its steps occurring in the mitochondria.
questions.why: The urea cycle spans two compartments. Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and formation of citrulline occur in mitochondria. The later three reactions that convert citrulline to urea and regenerate ornithine occur in the cytosol.

notes.A: Only two of the usual five reactions occur in mitochondria. They do not make up the majority of the steps.
notes.B: The mitochondrial count is two, not four, and the later reactions occur in the cytosol.
notes.C: The assertion about predominant mitochondrial location is incorrect because most of the standard reactions are cytosolic.
notes.D: The proposed count is incorrect. Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and citrulline formation are the two mitochondrial reactions.

questions.stem:
The metabolic fate of oxaloacetate includes:
I. condensing with acetyl CoA and committing to TCA cycle
II. conversion to glucose
III. conversion to aspartate.
questions.why: Oxaloacetate can condense with acetyl-CoA to form citrate, provide gluconeogenic carbon after conversion to phosphoenolpyruvate, or accept an amino group to form aspartate. Its fate depends on tissue and metabolic state.

notes.A: Citrate formation is one fate, but oxaloacetate can also support glucose synthesis or be transaminated to aspartate.
notes.B: Condensation and gluconeogenesis are valid. Aspartate aminotransferase also converts oxaloacetate to aspartate.
notes.C: Glucose synthesis and aspartate formation are possible, and citrate synthase also uses oxaloacetate as a substrate.
notes.D: Citrate and aspartate are valid products. Oxaloacetate can also supply carbon for gluconeogenesis.

questions.stem:
The generation of ammonia in the reaction catalysed by glutamate dehydrogenase:
I. requires the participation of NAD+ or NADP+
II. may be reversed to consume ammonia when present in excess
III. is enhanced by increased ATP/ADP or GTP/GDP.
questions.why: Glutamate dehydrogenase can use NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ in oxidative deamination, releasing ammonia and forming alpha-ketoglutarate. The reaction is reversible. High energy signals such as GTP generally inhibit oxidative deamination, while ADP can activate the enzyme.

notes.A: A pyridine nucleotide is used for oxidation, and the enzyme can also catalyse the reverse reaction under suitable conditions.
notes.C: The reaction is reversible, but a high-energy state does not generally stimulate oxidative deamination. The nucleotide acceptor is also required.
notes.D: NAD⁺ or NADP⁺ can support oxidative deamination. High GTP inhibits the enzyme rather than providing the proposed stimulation.
notes.E: The first two statements describe cofactor use and reversibility. The claim about stimulation by a high ATP or GTP state is the error.

questions.stem:
The accumulation of ammonia may lead to the following:
I. Impaired protein synthesis
II. Decreased synthesis of ATP
III. impaired impulse conduction.
questions.why: Excess ammonia can disrupt mitochondrial energy production and neurotransmission. In settings such as cirrhosis, hyperammonaemia can also impair skeletal muscle protein synthesis. The effects depend on the affected tissue and severity.

notes.A: Protein synthesis can be impaired, but energy metabolism and nervous system function can also be affected.
notes.B: Ammonia can alter protein synthesis and ATP metabolism, and disturbed neurotransmission is also an important feature of toxicity.
notes.C: Impaired energy production and neural signalling are recognised effects. Hyperammonaemia can also interfere with muscle protein synthesis.
notes.D: Ammonia can impair protein synthesis and neural function. It can additionally disrupt pathways that support ATP production.

questions.stem:
The carbon skeleton of cysteine is metabolised to:
I. pyruvate
II. taurine
III. glutathione
questions.why: Cysteine catabolism can yield pyruvate, and oxidative pathways through cysteinesulfinate can yield taurine. Glutathione also contains cysteine, but synthesis incorporates the intact amino acid rather than degrading its carbon skeleton.

notes.A: Pyruvate is one product of cysteine degradation. Cysteine can also provide the carbon backbone for taurine.
notes.C: Taurine can be made from cysteine. Glutathione synthesis uses intact cysteine, rather than catabolising the skeleton to glutathione.
notes.D: Pyruvate can result from cysteine catabolism, whereas glutathione is assembled from intact amino acid residues. Taurine is also a valid fate.
notes.E: This group mixes products of cysteine catabolism with a peptide formed by incorporation of intact cysteine.

questions.stem:
The components of folic acid are:
I. para-amino benzoic acid
II. substituted pteridine
III. glutamine.
questions.why: Folic acid contains a substituted pteridine ring joined to para-aminobenzoic acid and a glutamate residue. The amino acid component is glutamic acid rather than glutamine.

notes.A: Para-aminobenzoic acid is a component, but folic acid also contains a substituted pteridine ring.
notes.C: The pteridine component is present. The attached amino acid is glutamate, not its amide glutamine.
notes.D: Para-aminobenzoic acid is present, but glutamine is not the amino acid component. This combination also omits the pteridine ring.
notes.E: The ring and para-aminobenzoic acid are correct components. Adding glutamine makes the combination inaccurate.

questions.stem:
The following groups of amino acids are purely glycogenic:
I. serine, alanine, threonine
II. aspartate, cysteine, histidine
III. isoleucine, asparagine, threonine.
questions.why: Serine, alanine, aspartate, cysteine, histidine are glycogenic. Threonine and isoleucine are both.

notes.A: Leaves out II, which is also true.
notes.C: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes III, which is false.

questions.stem:
The following amino acids are both glycogenic and ketogenic:
I. isoleucine
II. tyrosine
III. serine.
questions.why: Isoleucine yields acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA, while tyrosine yields acetoacetate and fumarate. Each supplies both ketogenic and glucogenic products. Serine is glucogenic through its conversion to pyruvate.

notes.A: Isoleucine is mixed, but tyrosine also supplies both a ketogenic product and a glucogenic product.
notes.C: Tyrosine is mixed, whereas serine yields pyruvate as a glucogenic product. This grouping also leaves out isoleucine.
notes.D: Serine is not conventionally ketogenic. Tyrosine is a mixed amino acid and is missing from this grouping.
notes.E: Isoleucine and tyrosine belong in the mixed group. Serine is classified as glucogenic.

questions.stem:
The carbon skeletons of the following amino acids are converted to acetyl CoA:
I. tyrosine
II. isoleucine
III. tryptophan.
questions.why: Isoleucine breakdown yields acetyl-CoA directly. Tryptophan can yield acetoacetyl-CoA and tyrosine yields acetoacetate. Their ketogenic products can give rise to acetyl-CoA during further metabolism, although the immediate breakdown products differ.

notes.A: Tyrosine provides an indirect route through acetoacetate, but isoleucine and tryptophan also provide ketogenic carbon.
notes.B: Isoleucine yields acetyl-CoA and tryptophan yields a ketogenic product. Tyrosine also supplies ketogenic carbon through acetoacetate.
notes.C: Tyrosine and tryptophan supply ketogenic products. Isoleucine provides acetyl-CoA directly as well.
notes.D: This pair gives two examples, but tryptophan also provides ketogenic carbon through acetoacetyl-CoA.

questions.stem:
Polar uncharged amino acids:
I. Serine
II. Cysteine
III. Methionine.
questions.why: Serine and cysteine have uncharged polar side chains under usual physiological conditions. Serine has a hydroxyl group and cysteine a thiol group. Methionine has a thioether and is conventionally grouped with nonpolar amino acids.

notes.A: Serine is polar and uncharged, but cysteine also belongs in this category.
notes.C: Cysteine belongs in the polar uncharged group. Methionine's thioether side chain is usually classified as nonpolar.
notes.D: Serine is polar and uncharged, whereas methionine is grouped with nonpolar residues. Cysteine is missing.
notes.E: Cysteine and serine have polar functional groups. Methionine is excluded because its side chain is conventionally nonpolar.

questions.stem:
The following are polar positively charged amino acids:
I. arginine
II. glutamine
III. glutamate.
questions.why: Arginine has a guanidinium side chain that remains positively charged at physiological pH. Glutamine has an uncharged amide side chain, while glutamate carries a negative side-chain charge.

notes.B: Arginine is positive, but glutamine's side-chain amide has no net charge at physiological pH.
notes.C: Glutamine is uncharged and glutamate is negatively charged. Neither belongs to the basic, positively charged group.
notes.D: Glutamate has a carboxylate side chain and is negatively charged, unlike the guanidinium group of arginine.
notes.E: All three side chains are polar, but only arginine is positively charged under ordinary physiological conditions.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Unusual amino acids result from modifications of the common amino acids.
Reason: Unusual amino acids have no genetic coding for their biosynthesizing enzymes.
questions.why: Many unusual residues in proteins come from modification of a standard amino acid after translation. For example, prolyl hydroxylase acts on proline residues in collagen. The enzymes responsible for such modifications are themselves encoded by genes.

notes.A: The assertion applies to many modified residues, but their modifying enzymes do have genetic coding.
notes.B: Hydroxylation of proline illustrates the assertion. The reason is false because the modifying enzyme is encoded by DNA.
notes.D: The premise about modification is valid for residues such as hydroxyproline. The claim about absent coding for the enzymes is false.
notes.E: The reason is false, but post-translational modification of common amino acids is a recognised source of unusual residues.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Glutamate dehydrogenase is an allosteric enzyme.
Reason: Glutamate dehydrogenase activity is activated by high levels of GTP and ADP.
questions.why: Mammalian glutamate dehydrogenase is regulated allosterically. ADP can activate it, while GTP generally inhibits it. The reason incorrectly assigns the same effect to both nucleotides.

notes.A: Both nucleotides affect the enzyme, but GTP is an inhibitory signal rather than an activator.
notes.B: The reason is inaccurate because the directions of GTP and ADP regulation differ.
notes.D: The enzyme is demonstrably allosteric, and the proposed activation by high GTP is incorrect.
notes.E: The assertion is supported by nucleotide regulation. The error is the stated effect of GTP.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Pyridoxal phosphate serves a prosthetic group in the transfer an amino group to an α-keto acid.
Reason: Pyridoxal phosphate serves as coenzyme tightly bound to transaminase.
questions.why: Aminotransferases use tightly bound pyridoxal phosphate as a prosthetic group. It temporarily accepts an amino group to form pyridoxamine phosphate, then transfers the group to an alpha-keto acid and regenerates pyridoxal phosphate.

notes.B: Tight association with the aminotransferase is consistent with its role as the enzyme's prosthetic group during amino transfer.
notes.C: Pyridoxal phosphate is indeed a tightly associated coenzyme of these transaminases, making the reason true.
notes.D: The assertion is true because pyridoxal phosphate participates directly in the two-stage transfer of the amino group.
notes.E: Both statements describe a recognised feature of pyridoxal phosphate-dependent aminotransferases.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Oxidative deamination reactions generate reducing equivalents for biosynthesis.
Reason: Oxidative deamination produces NADH as a byproduct.
questions.why: The reason is true: glutamate dehydrogenase uses NAD+ (or NADP+) and produces NADH when it deaminates glutamate. The assertion is false as stated: the NADH from oxidative deamination mainly feeds the electron transport chain for ATP, while biosynthesis uses NADPH, which glutamate dehydrogenase consumes in the reverse (reductive amination) direction.

notes.A: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.B: Wrong here: the assertion is false.
notes.C: Wrong here: the assertion is false and the reason is true.
notes.E: Wrong here: the reason is true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate belongs to the hydrolases.
Reason: fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is involved in aldol cleavage.
questions.why: Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a glycolytic metabolite. Aldolase cleaves its carbon–carbon bond to form glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate. The enzyme fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase performs a separate hydrolysis during gluconeogenesis.

notes.A: The metabolite is not an enzyme and therefore does not belong to the hydrolase class. It is a substrate for aldolase.
notes.B: The reason is correct, but the assertion confuses the metabolite with the enzyme that hydrolyses it.
notes.C: The assertion is false because fructose 1,6-bisphosphate is a substrate. Aldol cleavage of it does occur in glycolysis.
notes.E: The assertion is incorrect, but aldolase does cleave fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two triose phosphates.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Lysine is an essential amino acid.
Reason: lysine cannot be synthesized by the human body and must be obtained from the diet.
questions.why: Lysine is nutritionally essential in humans because there is no pathway that can synthesise enough lysine for normal needs. Dietary protein therefore supplies the lysine required for protein synthesis and other metabolic functions.

notes.B: Dependence on dietary supply is the basis for classifying lysine as an essential amino acid.
notes.C: Humans cannot make sufficient lysine endogenously, so the reason correctly explains its essential status.
notes.D: Lysine is an essential amino acid, making the assertion as well as the reason true.
notes.E: Both statements are supported by human nutritional requirements for lysine.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Fructose is absorbed directly into the bloodstream.
Reason: fructose is one of the dietary monosaccharides.
questions.why: Dietary fructose is already a monosaccharide and does not require digestion into smaller sugars. It enters intestinal epithelial cells chiefly through GLUT5 and exits toward portal blood chiefly through GLUT2.

notes.B: Being a monosaccharide explains why fructose can be absorbed without prior hydrolysis, though transport across enterocytes is still required.
notes.C: Fructose is a dietary monosaccharide. It is distinct from disaccharides such as sucrose that require hydrolysis.
notes.D: Fructose can reach portal blood after transport across intestinal cells, so the assertion is valid in the usual nutritional sense.
notes.E: The two statements describe a monosaccharide that can be absorbed without enzymatic digestion, using specific transporters.

questions.stem:
The urea cycle:
I. synthesis of carbamoyl phosphate is enhanced by amino acid ingestion
II. ornithine transcarbamoylase is also active in the cytosol of humans
III. the generation of a mole of urea requires the expenditure of four high-energy phosphate bonds
questions.why: A larger amino acid load increases the need to dispose of nitrogen through carbamoyl phosphate and urea. Ornithine transcarbamylase is mitochondrial in humans. Each urea requires three ATP molecules, equivalent to four high-energy phosphate bonds.

notes.A: The amino acid load can increase ureagenesis. The energy cost of four high-energy phosphate bonds is also correct.
notes.B: Carbamoyl phosphate synthesis responds to amino acid nitrogen load, but ornithine transcarbamylase is not a human cytosolic urea-cycle enzyme.
notes.C: The energy cost is correct. The location of ornithine transcarbamylase is mitochondrial, and amino acid intake can increase pathway flux.
notes.E: The cytosolic-location statement is false. Increased nitrogen disposal and the four-bond energy cost both apply.

questions.stem:
Ammonia is toxic because:
I. it inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase system
II. it reverses the glutamate dehydrogenase reaction
III. it impedes synthesis of the neurotransmitter gamma-aminobutyric acid
questions.why: Excess ammonia drives glutamate dehydrogenase backwards, draining α-ketoglutarate from the TCA cycle and cutting ATP production (II). It also diverts glutamate into glutamine, reducing GABA synthesis (III), and NH4+ competes with K+ at the Na+/K+-ATPase, disturbing neuronal membranes (I).

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Phenylketonuria:
I. the characteristic slight dilution of skin and hair pigmentation is due to a defective phenylalanine hydroxylase
II. may be characterized by high levels of phenylpyruvic acid in the urine of affected subjects
III. may be due to deficiency in tetrahydrobiopterin.
questions.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency can cause phenylalanine accumulation, urinary phenylketones and reduced pigmentation from altered tyrosine and melanin metabolism. Tetrahydrobiopterin disorders can also produce hyperphenylalaninaemia by limiting a cofactor required by the hydroxylase.

notes.A: Impaired phenylalanine hydroxylation can affect pigmentation, but phenylpyruvate excretion and cofactor-related disorders are also pertinent.
notes.B: Hypopigmentation and phenylketonuria fit classic hydroxylase deficiency. A shortage of tetrahydrobiopterin can also limit hydroxylation.
notes.C: Both phenylketones and cofactor defects are relevant, and pigmentation can be lighter in untreated classic disease.
notes.D: Pigmentation and tetrahydrobiopterin are relevant. The abnormal phenylalanine pool can also generate urinary phenylpyruvate.

questions.stem: In a child's urine were detected phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate. What enzyme insufficiency causes this?
questions.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine. Deficiency leads to excess phenylalanine, some of which is metabolised to phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate.

notes.A: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinaemia type I and accumulation of metabolites such as succinylacetone.
notes.B: Tyrosine 3-monooxygenase makes L-DOPA in catecholamine synthesis. Its deficiency does not explain accumulation of phenylketones.
notes.D: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency disrupts homocysteine metabolism. It is unrelated to the phenylalanine hydroxylation step.

questions.stem:
Which of these amino acids can result in maple syrup disease during catabolism of their carbon chain:
I. Leucine
II. Valine
III. isoleucine
questions.why: Leucine, valine and isoleucine are first converted to their corresponding branched-chain alpha-keto acids. Maple syrup urine disease impairs the shared dehydrogenase complex that normally processes all three.

notes.A: Leucine is affected, but the same dehydrogenase complex processes the products of valine and isoleucine catabolism.
notes.B: Leucine and valine belong to the affected group. Isoleucine also requires the shared enzyme complex.
notes.C: Valine and isoleucine are relevant, but leucine metabolism is also disrupted and is especially important in the disease.
notes.D: Leucine and isoleucine are affected. Valine generates a third branched-chain keto acid processed by the same complex.

questions.stem:
Intermittent branch chain ketonuria is characterized by:
I. symptoms appearing early in life
II. variant of maple syrup urine disease
III. deficiency in α-keto dehydrogenase complex:
questions.why: It is a variant of MSUD (ii) caused by the enzyme deficiency (iii), but symptoms appear intermittently, often later.

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II and III, which are true.
notes.B: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.D: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes I, which is false.

questions.stem:
Tyrosinaemia is characterized by the following:
I. type III tyrosinaemia is associated with the deficiency of parahydroxy phenylpyruvate dioxygenase
II. type I tyrosinaemia is associated with increased susceptibility to hepatorenal disease and hepatic cancers
III. type II tyrosinaemia is associated with the deficiency of fumarylacetoacetase.
questions.why: Type III tyrosinaemia results from 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase deficiency. Type I causes hepatorenal disease and increases liver cancer risk because fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase is deficient. Type II instead results from tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency.

notes.A: The enzyme defect in type III is correctly described. Type I also carries the stated hepatic and renal risks.
notes.C: The type I complications are correct. Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency belongs to type I, rather than type II.
notes.D: Type III involves the dioxygenase. Type II involves tyrosine aminotransferase, and this grouping leaves out the characteristic type I complications.
notes.E: The descriptions of types I and III are correct, but the enzyme assigned to type II actually belongs to type I.

questions.stem:
Tyrosinaemia type II is associated with:
I. intellectual disability
II. eye and skin lesions
III. seizures.
questions.why: Tyrosinaemia type II results from tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency. Characteristic findings include painful eye lesions and thickened skin on the palms or soles. Some affected people also have intellectual disability. Seizures are more characteristic of type III.

notes.A: Intellectual disability can occur, but the eye and skin findings are particularly characteristic of type II.
notes.C: Eye and skin lesions fit type II. Seizures are more characteristic of type III, and intellectual disability is also possible in type II.
notes.D: Intellectual disability can be associated with type II. The characteristic combination also includes corneal and skin lesions, not seizures.
notes.E: The first two features fit the typical type II description. Seizures do not belong to its defining clinical pattern.

questions.stem:
Deficiency of the following enzymes may be characterized by the following:
I. ornithine transcarbamylase and citrullinaemia
II. argininosuccinate lyase and argininosuccinic aciduria
III. carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and hyperammonaemia.
questions.why: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinic aciduria, and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency causes hyperammonaemia. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency impairs citrulline formation and is associated with low or inappropriately normal citrulline, rather than citrullinaemia.

notes.A: The early ornithine transcarbamylase block reduces citrulline formation. Citrullinaemia is typically associated with argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency.
notes.B: Argininosuccinic aciduria does result from the lyase defect, but ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency does not typically raise citrulline.
notes.D: Hyperammonaemia occurs with the carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I defect. The ornithine transcarbamylase pairing remains incorrect.
notes.E: The final two pairings are valid. The first pairing incorrectly associates ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency with citrulline accumulation.

questions.stem:
Cystathionuria is associated with the following:
I. reduced affinity of cystathionine y lyase
II. deficiency of biotin
III. deficiency of cystathionine β synthase.
questions.why: Cystathionuria is caused by a defect in cystathionine gamma-lyase (i).

notes.B: Includes II, which is false.
notes.C: Includes II and III, which are false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false.
notes.E: Includes II and III, which are false.

questions.stem:
Homocystinuria is caused by:
I. methionine synthase
II. pyridoxal phosphate
III. deficiency of cystathionine β synthase.
questions.why: Defects in methionine synthase, lack of PLP, and CBS deficiency can all lead to homocystinuria.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Isovaleryl acidemia is characterized by:
I. speech defects
II. it is associated with mild mental retardation
III. cheesy odour.
questions.why: Isovaleric acidemia causes speech defects, mild intellectual disability, and a distinct 'sweaty feet' odor.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Inborn errors of metabolism:
I. maybe manifested early in life
II. maybe manifested later in life
III. dependent on external factors.
questions.why: Inborn errors of metabolism are genetic, but their age of presentation varies with residual function and physiological demands. Some present in the newborn period, while others emerge later or become apparent during illness, fasting or a particular dietary exposure.

notes.A: Some disorders present early, but residual enzyme activity can delay the first symptoms until childhood or adulthood.
notes.B: The age at presentation can vary. External stresses such as illness or fasting may also trigger decompensation.
notes.C: Later onset and environmental triggers are possible, but severe defects can also cause symptoms shortly after birth.
notes.D: Environmental exposures can influence presentation, and inherited disorders can first manifest either early or later in life.

questions.stem:
The biochemical consequences of metabolic block involve:
I. Reduction in substrate concentration
II. Interference with feedback mechanism
III. Reduced formation of product.
questions.why: A block usually leads to accumulation of the immediate substrate and reduced production of the expected product. Loss of the product can alter feedback control, and accumulated substrate may be diverted into alternative pathways.

notes.A: The immediate substrate usually accumulates rather than becoming depleted when the enzyme cannot process it.
notes.B: Feedback can be altered, but reduced substrate is not the typical result immediately before the block.
notes.D: Product formation may fall, but the substrate immediately upstream of the defect ordinarily rises.
notes.E: Reduced product and altered feedback are plausible. The general claim that the immediate substrate decreases reverses the expected effect.

questions.stem:
Initial specimen for detection of inborn errors of metabolism:
I. red cell haemolysates
II. skin biopsies
III. urine.
questions.why: All can be used depending on the suspected disorder.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Specimen for prenatal screening for inborn error of metabolism include:
I. Chorionic villus sample
II. Amniotic fluid
III. Liver biopsy.
questions.why: Chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis can provide fetal or placental material for targeted prenatal assessment of selected inherited metabolic disorders. The choice depends on gestational timing, the familial variant and the proposed assay.

notes.A: Chorionic villi can provide DNA or cells, and amniotic-fluid sampling can also provide fetal cells or relevant metabolites.
notes.C: Amniotic fluid is useful, but liver biopsy is not a standard prenatal specimen for this purpose.
notes.D: Chorionic villi can be sampled for targeted diagnosis. Amniotic fluid is another standard option rather than fetal liver tissue.
notes.E: The recognised routine options in this comparison are chorionic villi and amniotic fluid. Fetal liver biopsy is not routinely used.

questions.stem:
Neonatal screening for inborn error focuses on a disease:
I. Relatively common in the population
II. Treatable
III. Easily tested.
questions.why: A newborn screening programme weighs disease burden, the benefit of early treatment and the availability of a practical and reliable test. Frequency is considered in the target population, although rare conditions can be included when early detection has substantial benefit.

notes.A: Frequency and population impact matter, but screening also requires a useful test and a benefit from identifying the condition early.
notes.B: Treatability and public-health impact are relevant. A feasible and reliable screening method is another major requirement.
notes.C: The value of a practicable test and effective early treatment is assessed together with population burden and programme resources.
notes.D: A simple test and a significant population burden alone are insufficient. A useful early intervention or demonstrable benefit also matters.

questions.stem:
Late clinical findings of inborn errors of metabolism may include:
I. Failure to thrive
II. Persistent jaundice
III. Intellectual disability.
questions.why: Inherited metabolic disease can impair growth, damage the liver or affect the developing nervous system. Failure to thrive, persistent jaundice and intellectual disability may therefore emerge over time, depending on the underlying disorder.

notes.A: Poor growth can occur, but persistent jaundice or later neurodevelopmental difficulties may also be clues.
notes.B: Growth failure and jaundice can reflect systemic and hepatic involvement. Some disorders also cause later developmental impairment.
notes.C: Persistent jaundice and intellectual disability can occur. Poor weight gain is another possible longer-term finding.
notes.D: Growth and developmental difficulties are compatible, but persistent jaundice can also signal hepatic involvement.

questions.stem:
Routine laboratory investigations for inborn error of metabolism related acid-base disturbance:
I. Blood gases
II. Bicarbonate
III. Plasma ammonia.
questions.why: A blood gas and bicarbonate help characterise the acid–base disorder. Plasma ammonia is a complementary urgent metabolic test in a suspected inborn error, since hyperammonaemia can occur in urea cycle disorders or secondarily in some organic acidaemias.

notes.A: Blood gases define pH and the respiratory component. Bicarbonate and ammonia can add information about metabolic disturbance and possible cause.
notes.B: Blood gases and bicarbonate characterise the acid–base pattern, while ammonia can identify an important accompanying abnormality.
notes.C: Bicarbonate and ammonia are useful, but blood gases help distinguish respiratory from metabolic disturbances.
notes.D: Blood gases and ammonia are relevant. The bicarbonate concentration also helps quantify the metabolic component.

questions.stem:
Management of inborn errors of metabolism focuses on:
I. Limiting precursors in affected pathway
II. Reduce the accumulated products
III. Supply the deficient enzyme.
questions.why: Treatment depends on the biochemical defect. Strategies can include reducing intake of a precursor, removing or diverting a toxic accumulated metabolite, and supplying an enzyme when effective replacement exists.

notes.A: Substrate restriction can reduce flux through a blocked pathway, but other disorders require metabolite removal or enzyme replacement.
notes.B: Lowering precursors and accumulated substances are recognised approaches. Some conditions also have approved enzyme replacement therapy.
notes.C: Removing accumulated substances and replacing an enzyme can help in selected disorders. Precursor restriction is also used.
notes.D: Restricting a precursor or replacing an enzyme can help, but lowering toxic metabolites directly is another recognised strategy.

questions.stem:
Classic galactosaemia is as a result of a defect in the enzyme:
I. Galactokinase
II. UDP-galactose-4-epimerase
III. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase.
questions.why: Classic galactosaemia is caused by deficient galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase, or GALT. Galactose-1-phosphate cannot be metabolised normally and accumulates when affected infants receive dietary galactose.

notes.A: Galactokinase deficiency causes a different form of galactosaemia and is especially associated with cataracts.
notes.B: Galactokinase and UDP-galactose 4-epimerase deficiencies are distinct disorders, rather than the enzyme defect in classical disease.
notes.C: GALT is the enzyme deficient in classic galactosaemia. Epimerase deficiency is a separate biochemical diagnosis.
notes.D: Adding galactokinase deficiency mixes two distinct disorders. Classic galactosaemia results from the GALT defect alone.

questions.stem:
Precursor amino acids in the inborn error of metabolism methyl malonic aciduria:
I. Isoleucine
II. Leucine
III. Serine.
questions.why: Isoleucine breakdown can yield propionyl-CoA, which normally passes through methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. Leucine is ketogenic and does not provide propionyl-CoA, while serine is usually degraded to pyruvate.

notes.B: Isoleucine is a precursor, but leucine breakdown yields ketogenic products without contributing propionyl-CoA.
notes.C: Neither leucine nor serine is a usual propionyl-CoA precursor. This grouping omits isoleucine.
notes.D: Isoleucine can feed the pathway, but serine normally contributes carbon through pyruvate rather than propionyl-CoA.
notes.E: Of the listed amino acids, only isoleucine supplies a propionyl-CoA precursor to the methylmalonyl-CoA pathway.

questions.stem:
These conditions are due to mutations in transport proteins:
I. Menkes syndrome
II. Cystinosis
III. Thalassaemia.
questions.why: Menkes syndrome involves ATP7A, a copper-transporting ATPase. Cystinosis involves cystinosin, which exports cystine from lysosomes. Thalassaemia results from reduced synthesis of a globin chain rather than a defective membrane transporter.

notes.A: The Menkes defect is in a copper transporter, and cystinosis also results from abnormal membrane transport.
notes.C: Cystinosis is a transport disorder, but thalassaemia affects globin production and does not belong in this pair.
notes.D: Menkes syndrome involves ATP7A. Thalassaemia involves globin genes, while the omitted cystinosis option is also a transport disorder.
notes.E: Both Menkes syndrome and cystinosis involve transport proteins. Thalassaemia changes the quantity of globin made.

questions.stem:
Inborn errors of metabolism caused by mutation in hormonal receptor genes:
I. Dwarfism
II. Vitamin D dependent ricket
III. Testicular feminization.
questions.why: All can result from receptor mutations.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Assertion: PKU, MSUD and alkaptonuria are inheritable disease.
Reason: PKU, MSUD and alkaptonuria are caused by defects in protein metabolism.
questions.why: Phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease and alkaptonuria can be inherited through pathogenic variants in enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism. The affected pathway explains the metabolic phenotype. The inherited variants explain the familial transmission.

notes.A: The amino acid pathway defects describe the biochemical class. Inheritance is due to pathogenic genetic variants, rather than being proved by that classification.
notes.C: The reason is broadly true when protein metabolism refers to amino acid degradation and processing.
notes.D: The assertion is correct because these disorders can be transmitted as inherited metabolic conditions.
notes.E: Both statements are broadly correct. Not every acquired disturbance of amino acid metabolism is inherited, so the pathway category alone does not explain transmission.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Histidinaemia is associated with elevated blood, CSF and urinary excretion of histidine and its metabolites.
Reason: Histidinaemia is characterized by decreased concentration of urocanic acid in blood and skin.
questions.why: Histidase normally converts histidine to urocanate. In histidinaemia, deficient activity allows histidine and some metabolites to accumulate while urocanate production falls. The low product and high substrate arise from the same enzyme defect.

notes.A: Reduced urocanate is a downstream sign of the defect. It does not itself cause histidine to accumulate.
notes.C: The reason correctly identifies reduced formation of urocanate, the product of the histidase reaction.
notes.D: Histidine accumulation is a recognised feature, so the assertion should not be rejected.
notes.E: Both changes are compatible with deficient histidase activity. They describe opposite sides of the same metabolic block.

questions.stem: A result of mutation in gene coding for the enzyme that catalysis a deamination process in haem synthesis.
questions.why: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by deficient hydroxymethylbilane synthase, also known as porphobilinogen deaminase. This enzyme joins four porphobilinogen molecules to make a linear precursor of haem and releases ammonia in the process.

notes.A: Retinoblastoma involves loss of RB1 tumour-suppressor function, not a haem-pathway enzyme.
notes.B: Retinitis pigmentosa comprises inherited retinal degeneration disorders and is not caused by porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency.
notes.D: Achondroplasia results from altered FGFR3 growth signalling, not a haem biosynthetic defect.
notes.E: Cystinosis involves impaired export of cystine from lysosomes rather than a block in porphyrin synthesis.

questions.stem: Caused by mutation of protein involved in cellular growth control.
questions.why: Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the RB tumor suppressor gene.

notes.B: This is a photoreceptor defect.
notes.C: This is a haem synthesis enzyme defect.
notes.D: FGFR3 is a growth-factor receptor; RB is the classic growth-control (tumour-suppressor) protein.
notes.E: This is a transporter defect.

questions.stem:
Tay Sachs disease presents with:
I. Muscle weakness
II. Patient presents with diminished muscle tone
III. Deterioration of cognitive processes.
questions.why: Tay–Sachs disease results from deficient hexosaminidase A activity and accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neurons. Progressive neurodegeneration can cause muscle weakness, reduced tone early in the course and loss of developmental or cognitive abilities.

notes.A: Weakness is common, but loss of tone and progressive neurological decline can also occur.
notes.B: Weakness and hypotonia are compatible with infantile disease. Loss of developmental or cognitive function is also characteristic as it progresses.
notes.C: Hypotonia and regression are recognised. Progressive loss of muscle strength is another manifestation.
notes.D: Weakness and cognitive deterioration are consistent with the disease. Early hypotonia can contribute to the motor presentation.

questions.stem:
In osteogenesis imperfecta:
I. The gene COL1A1 is implicated
II. Triple helix formation is slow
III. Cross-linking of protein fiber is compact.
questions.why: Variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2 can cause osteogenesis imperfecta by reducing type I collagen quantity or altering its structure. Glycine substitutions within the triple-helical region can slow folding. More compact cross-linking is not a general hallmark.

notes.A: COL1A1 is implicated, and structural collagen variants can also delay triple-helix formation.
notes.C: Some variants slow folding, but compact cross-linking is not a defining feature. This group also omits COL1A1 involvement.
notes.D: COL1A1 involvement is correct, but unusually compact cross-linking is not the typical explanation for collagen fragility.
notes.E: The gene and folding statements fit structural collagen defects. The cross-linking claim is not a recognised general feature.

questions.stem:
α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex is synonymous to:
I. pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
II. glutamate dehydrogenase
III. malate dehydrogenase.
questions.why: The alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex usually refers to the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

notes.B: Includes II, which is false.
notes.C: Includes II and III, which are false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false.
notes.E: Includes II and III, which are false.

questions.stem:
Phenylketonuria:
I. incidence of 1:100,000 live births
II. associated with light hair, eye and skin
III. an autosomal recessive condition.
questions.why: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is autosomal recessive. Untreated disease can reduce pigmentation through effects on tyrosine and melanin metabolism. Its incidence varies by population, so a fixed value of one in 100,000 is not a general estimate.

notes.A: Incidence varies widely between populations. The mode of inheritance and possible hypopigmentation are better general features.
notes.B: Lighter pigmentation can occur, but the proposed fixed frequency is not reliable across populations.
notes.D: Autosomal recessive inheritance is correct. The stated incidence is not general, and reduced pigmentation can also be seen.
notes.E: Pigmentation and inheritance fit typical descriptions, but the proposed universal incidence is not supported.

questions.stem: A hormonal (growth-factor receptor) defect.
questions.why: Achondroplasia is caused by activating variants in FGFR3, a fibroblast growth factor receptor. Increased signalling inhibits normal growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and affects endochondral bone growth.

notes.A: Retinoblastoma usually results from loss of RB1 tumour-suppressor activity. RB1 is not a growth-factor receptor.
notes.B: Retinitis pigmentosa can result from defects in phototransduction or other photoreceptor functions, rather than a typical FGFR3 growth-signalling defect.
notes.C: Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by deficient activity of a haem biosynthetic enzyme rather than a growth-factor receptor.
notes.E: Cystinosis involves a lysosomal cystine transporter, rather than a receptor that regulates bone growth.

questions.stem: Involves a defect in a light-sensitive receptor.
questions.why: One form of retinitis pigmentosa results from variants in rhodopsin, the light-sensitive receptor of rod photoreceptors. Other genes can also cause the retinal degeneration, so rhodopsin is an example rather than the cause of every case.

notes.A: Retinoblastoma is a retinal tumour caused by cell-cycle control defects rather than a photopigment receptor defect.
notes.C: Acute intermittent porphyria involves a haem biosynthetic enzyme and does not directly affect a light receptor.
notes.D: Achondroplasia involves a fibroblast growth factor receptor, which responds to signalling proteins rather than light.
notes.E: Cystinosis involves transport of cystine across lysosomal membranes and is not a phototransduction disorder.

questions.stem: The formation of porphobilinogen:
questions.why: Two molecules of delta-aminolaevulinic acid are condensed by ALA dehydratase to form porphobilinogen. This reaction occurs in the cytosol and precedes joining of four porphobilinogen units later in haem synthesis.

notes.A: Porphobilinogen deaminase uses porphobilinogen as substrate. It joins four units into hydroxymethylbilane.
notes.C: Formation of one porphobilinogen requires two ALA molecules. Four porphobilinogens are used in the later tetrapyrrole step.
notes.D: ALA is produced in mitochondria, then moves into the cytosol for conversion to porphobilinogen.

notes.B: Reducing equivalents for this oxygenase system are supplied by NADPH through a reductase, rather than principally by NADH.

notes.B: Porphin has an extended conjugated system and is not a highly saturated ring.
notes.C: Each of the four smaller rings is a pyrrole ring with one nitrogen, rather than an imidazole ring with two.
notes.D: Ferrous iron coordinates with the porphyrin ring in haem. The parent porphin molecule does not require a central metal.

questions.stem: The porphyrins are derived from porphin which:
questions.why: The porphin ring has four pyrrole units joined by four methene bridges. The bridge carbons participate in the conjugated macrocycle. Substituted porphyrins have additional side chains on that framework.

notes.A: Methyl groups are substituents on some porphyrins, such as protoporphyrin IX. They are not features of unsubstituted porphin.
notes.B: Methylene bridges are characteristic of reduced porphyrinogens. Porphin is the oxidised conjugated parent macrocycle.
notes.D: Porphin is a closed macrocycle. Linear tetrapyrroles arise when the ring is opened, as in haem degradation.

notes.A: Protoporphyrin IX also has two propionate groups. The methyl and vinyl groups do not account for all its substituents.
notes.C: Porphyrins are generally coloured because their conjugated rings absorb light. The reduced porphyrinogens are much less coloured.
notes.D: The ring system absorbs strongly, including a near-violet absorption band known as the Soret band.

notes.C: Coproporphyrins also have four conventional isomer types, with methyl and propionate side chains.

questions.stem: The following are features of acute intermittent porphyria:

notes.B: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency or inhibition is associated with porphyria cutanea tarda, rather than acute intermittent porphyria.
notes.D: Acute intermittent porphyria is classically detected through increased porphobilinogen and ALA during attacks, rather than urinary accumulation of uroporphyrinogen.

questions.why: Porphyria cutanea tarda arises when hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity is low. Accumulated porphyrins can absorb light and generate reactive species in exposed skin, causing fragility and blistering photosensitivity.

notes.B: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria. Porphyria cutanea tarda instead involves uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.
notes.D: Neurovisceral attacks characterise the acute hepatic porphyrias. Porphyria cutanea tarda predominantly affects light-exposed skin.

options.label: A

notes.A: Haemin is a ferric haem derivative and can form by oxidation. Enzymatic haem breakdown instead forms biliverdin, iron and carbon monoxide.
notes.B: Haem represses hepatic ALA synthase 1 expression and mitochondrial import rather than enhancing them.
notes.D: In erythroid cells, haem inhibits the haem-regulated kinase HRI, helping prevent inhibitory phosphorylation of eIF2α and supporting globin translation.

notes.A: A carboxylase adds a carboxyl group. This enzyme removes carboxyl carbons during oxidative decarboxylation.
notes.C: The physiological product is protoporphyrinogen IX, rather than a type IV product.
