questions.stem:
The allosteric manifestations of haemoglobin include:
I. Co-operative binding of O2
II. The sigmoidal nature of the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve
III. Conformational changes in structure brought about by a lowering of pH
questions.why: Oxygen binding changes haemoglobin's quaternary conformation and increases affinity at the remaining sites. This positive cooperativity makes the saturation curve sigmoidal. Lower pH stabilises lower-affinity states, contributing to the Bohr effect.

notes.A: Cooperative oxygen binding is one manifestation, but the curve shape and response to pH also reflect linked conformational changes.
notes.B: Cooperativity and the sigmoid curve are related. The pH-dependent shift also reflects allosteric coupling.
notes.C: The curve and response to pH show allostery, and the increase in affinity at other sites after oxygen binds is another example.
notes.D: Oxygen binding and pH influence conformation. Cooperative binding is also what gives the oxygen saturation curve its characteristic sigmoid shape.

questions.stem:
The oxygen dissociation curves for myoglobin and haemoglobin show that:
I. Myoglobin is more saturated with oxygen at any given PO2
II. The myoglobin curve always lies to the right of the haemoglobin curve
III. The haemoglobin curve has a sigmoid shape
questions.why: Myoglobin is a single-chain oxygen-binding protein with a high affinity and a hyperbolic saturation curve. Under comparable physiological conditions, its curve lies to the left of haemoglobin's. Haemoglobin has a sigmoid curve because its four binding sites interact cooperatively.

notes.A: Myoglobin binds oxygen at relatively low pressures. The comparison also includes the sigmoid shape of cooperative haemoglobin binding.
notes.B: Myoglobin is generally more saturated at the same physiological oxygen pressure, which places its curve to the left rather than to the right.
notes.C: Haemoglobin has a sigmoid curve, but myoglobin's higher affinity shifts its curve to lower oxygen pressures.
notes.E: The statements about higher saturation and the sigmoid curve are correct. The stated rightward position of the myoglobin curve is reversed.

questions.stem:
The functions of the polypeptide chain in haemoglobin include:
I. prevention of oxidation of active site Fe2+ to Fe3+
II. decreasing the affinity of binding of carbon monoxide
III. buffering of H+ ions
questions.why: Globin encloses haem in a pocket that favours reversible oxygen binding and helps limit spontaneous iron oxidation. It reduces the relative preference for carbon monoxide compared with free haem. Ionisable groups on globin also buffer hydrogen ions.

notes.A: The pocket helps protect ferrous iron from oxidation, although methaemoglobin can still form. The chain also participates in ligand selectivity and buffering.
notes.B: Protection of haem and discrimination against carbon monoxide are functions of the pocket. Proton buffering by globin is another function.
notes.C: The globin chain buffers protons and changes ligand affinity. Its haem pocket also helps limit oxidation of the iron.
notes.D: The pocket limits oxidation and globin groups can bind hydrogen ions. The protein also decreases the relative carbon monoxide preference of haem.

questions.stem:
The following statements are true about myoglobin:
I. The first amino acid in helix A is designated A1, the second A2, and so forth.
II. The molecule has altogether 7 non-helical segments.
III. The N-terminal non-helical region is made up of two amino acid residues designated N1 and N2.
questions.why: Standard globin notation uses letters A through H for helices and numbers for positions within each helix, such as A1 and A2. Connectors and terminal regions have their own names. The seven interhelix connectors are not the only nonhelical regions if the ends are counted.

notes.B: The seven connectors between eight helices do not include terminal segments outside the helices.
notes.C: The statement about segment count omits the termini, and the terminal residues are designated separately from the helix positions.
notes.D: The A1 and A2 notation is correct. Globin diagrams conventionally use NA notation for the segment before helix A.
notes.E: The letter-and-number rule for helical residues is valid, but the other statements miscount or misname nonhelical regions.

questions.stem:
In myoglobin:
I. The N-terminal non-helical region is made up of two amino acid residues designated NA1 and NA2
II. The oxygen binding site is the sixth co-ordination position of the haem iron
III. The carboxyl terminal non-helical region comprises five amino acids termed H1 through to H5.
questions.why: The segment before helix A uses the globin designation NA, such as NA1 and NA2 in the conventional myoglobin diagram. Oxygen binds at the sixth coordination position of haem iron. Positions labelled H1 and onward belong to helix H itself.

notes.A: The NA notation is appropriate for residues before helix A, and the sixth coordination site is also correctly identified.
notes.C: Oxygen binds to sixth-coordinate iron. Residues after helix H use a terminal designation, rather than the numbering of helix H itself.
notes.D: The N-terminal labels are defensible in the conventional example. The C-terminal nonhelical residues do not use the H1 through H5 helix labels.
notes.E: The sixth iron coordination site binds oxygen, and the NA labels refer to the N-terminal segment. The C-terminal labels are the error.

questions.stem:
The following is true about the distribution of amino-acids in myoglobin:
I. The interior of myoglobin consists entirely of non-polar amino-acids
II. The interior of myoglobin has only two polar amino-acids
III. The interior of myoglobin consists of residues such as leucine, valine, methionine and phenylalanine.
questions.why: The interior is packed with hydrophobic residues such as leucine, valine, methionine and phenylalanine (III). It is almost, but not entirely, non-polar (I is false): the only polar residues inside are the two histidines (E7 and F8) at the haem pocket (II).

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II and III, which are true.
notes.B: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.D: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes I, which is false.

questions.stem:
Concerning amino acid distribution in myoglobin:
I. Side chains of glutamate, aspartate, glutamine, asparagine, lysine or arginine are abundant in the interior of myoglobin.
II. Residues that have both a polar and a non-polar part, such as threonine, tyrosine, and tryptophan are positioned such that their non-polar part points inward.
III. Only two polar residues are found in the interior of myoglobin
questions.why: Charged and polar side chains (Glu, Asp, Gln, Asn, Lys, Arg) are on the surface, so I is false. Amphipathic residues such as Thr, Tyr and Trp point their non-polar parts inward (II), and the only polar residues in the interior are the two histidines E7 and F8 (III).

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II and III, which are true.
notes.B: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.D: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes I, which is false.

questions.stem:
Interactions at the active site of haemoglobin:
I. The distal histidine and other residues surrounding the sixth co-ordination point block the formation of haem-oxygen-haem sandwiches
II. Amino acids surrounding the sixth co-ordination point stabilize the ferrous form of myoglobin.
III. The polypeptide chain in haemoglobin creates a hindered haem environment
questions.why: The globin pocket partly encloses haem and regulates ligand access. The proximal histidine coordinates the iron and the distal environment helps stabilise bound oxygen and limit reactions of free haem, including formation of bridged aggregates and oxidation.

notes.A: The pocket limits approach of another haem and also shapes the protein environment that stabilises functional ferrous haem.
notes.B: Shielding and stabilisation are appropriate features. Restricting haem–haem contact helps prevent reactions seen with free haem.
notes.C: Protection against haem aggregation and the hindered binding site are relevant. The surrounding residues also influence the redox stability of the iron.
notes.D: The pocket helps limit contact between haem groups and stabilises the local chemistry. It also restricts access and orientation of ligands.

questions.stem:
The following statements are true:
I. The affinity of free haem for carbon monoxide and oxygen is about the same
II. In myoglobin and haemoglobin, the binding affinity for CO is 200 times that of O2.
III. The hindered haem environment ensures a reduction in affinity for carbon monoxide and reversible binding of oxygen
questions.why: In myoglobin and haemoglobin, CO binds about 200 times more tightly than O2 (II). That is far less than free haem, which binds CO about 25 000 times more strongly than O2 (so I is false). The hindered pocket (distal histidine forcing a bent geometry) cuts CO affinity and lets O2 bind reversibly (III).

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II and III, which are true.
notes.B: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.D: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes I, which is false.

questions.stem:
An active site in haemoglobin:
I. Has histidine F8 attached
II. Has histidine E7 attached
III. Can bind CO2, O2 and CO
questions.why: Histidine F8 is the proximal histidine and directly coordinates haem iron at the fifth position. The distal histidine E7 lies near the ligand at the sixth position without attaching directly to iron. Oxygen and carbon monoxide bind iron, while carbon dioxide mainly forms carbamates on globin.

notes.B: Proximal histidine F8 coordinates the iron. Distal histidine E7 influences the ligand environment but is not directly bound to iron.
notes.C: Neither direct attachment of E7 nor physiological binding of carbon dioxide to the oxygen-binding iron site is correct.
notes.D: Histidine F8 is the axial protein ligand. Carbon dioxide binds chiefly to amino groups on globin, separately from the iron ligand site.
notes.E: The proximal histidine coordinates iron, but the distal histidine does not. Carbon dioxide also does not share the usual iron site used by oxygen.

questions.stem:
A haemoglobin active site:
I. Is modulated by histidine E7 and other surrounding amino acid side chains
II. Is not affected by binding of O2 to another binding site
III. Binds 2,3 BPG as it off loads O2
questions.why: The distal histidine and neighbouring side chains influence the haem ligand-binding site. The site's oxygen affinity also changes when oxygen binds to other subunits. The allosteric effector 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds in the central cavity away from haem.

notes.B: The distal pocket influences oxygen binding, but the other subunits affect it through cooperativity.
notes.C: Oxygen binding sites communicate through quaternary changes, and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds elsewhere on the tetramer.
notes.D: Distal histidine modulates the haem site. The site for 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate lies in the cavity between the beta chains.
notes.E: The first claim is correct. Cooperativity and a separate binding site for 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate make the other two claims incorrect.

questions.stem:
The following statements are true:
I. Myoglobin is a monomer
II. Examples of secondary structure of a protein include β-pleated sheets, reverse turns and type II trans helix
III. Myoglobin has both tertiary and quaternary structures
questions.why: Myoglobin is a monomer with a folded tertiary structure and no ordinary multimeric quaternary structure. Beta sheets, turns and the extended polyproline II helix are recognised backbone conformations in proteins, although myoglobin is predominantly alpha-helical.

notes.A: The single polypeptide forms a monomer. Proteins can also contain the stated local backbone conformations.
notes.C: The secondary structure examples are valid. Myoglobin has tertiary structure but lacks the multi-chain arrangement required for quaternary structure.
notes.D: Myoglobin is monomeric, so the claim of both tertiary and quaternary structure is incorrect.
notes.E: Beta sheets, reverse turns and polyproline II conformations can occur in proteins. The statement that myoglobin has quaternary structure is incorrect.

questions.stem:
The hindered haem environment ensures that:
I. Haemoglobin is not easily oxygenated
II. There is decreased affinity for CO2
III. There is reversible binding of O2
questions.why: The haem pocket creates an environment in which oxygen binds reversibly to ferrous iron. Surrounding residues modulate ligand binding, allowing haemoglobin to load oxygen in the lungs and unload it in tissues.

notes.A: Haemoglobin can readily bind oxygen under pulmonary conditions. The pocket supports reversible binding without making oxygen uptake generally difficult.
notes.B: Carbon dioxide is carried mostly as bicarbonate or binds to globin amino groups. Its affinity is not the direct effect of the oxygen-binding pocket.
notes.D: The pocket permits efficient oxygen uptake and release. It does not chiefly prevent oxygenation or regulate a carbon dioxide binding site at haem.
notes.E: Reversible oxygen binding is the supported function. The other claims misrepresent oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide binding.

questions.stem:
Conserved amino-acids in the haemoglobin polypeptide chain include:
I. Histidine E7
II. Histidine F8
III. Glycine B6
questions.why: Conventional globin alignments identify important conserved positions, including the proximal histidine F8, distal histidine E7 and glycine B6 in the human haemoglobin chains. Proximal histidine directly coordinates iron, while distal histidine influences ligand binding.

notes.A: Distal histidine is important, but proximal histidine and a conserved glycine position also belong to the standard globin comparison.
notes.B: The two histidines have distinct roles near haem. Glycine B6 is also a conserved position in the adult human chains.
notes.C: Proximal histidine and glycine are relevant. The distal histidine is another conserved feature of the usual human globin pocket.
notes.D: Distal histidine and glycine are included, but this omits the proximal histidine that directly coordinates haem iron.

questions.stem:
The allosteric properties of haemoglobin include:
I. Co-operative binding of O2
II. Conformational changes in structure brought about by increase in [H+]
III. The non-sigmoidal nature of the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve
questions.why: Cooperative oxygen binding gives haemoglobin a sigmoid dissociation curve. Increasing hydrogen ion concentration stabilises lower-affinity states through the Bohr effect. Both changes illustrate coupling between binding and conformation.

notes.A: Cooperative binding is an example, and changes in proton concentration can also shift haemoglobin conformation.
notes.C: The proton effect is correct, but the oxygen saturation curve is sigmoid rather than nonsigmoid.
notes.D: Positive cooperativity causes sigmoid behaviour. This pairing also omits the conformation change associated with higher hydrogen ion concentration.
notes.E: Oxygen and proton responses are both allosteric. The statement denying the sigmoid shape remains false.

questions.stem:
The allosteric properties of haemoglobin include:
I. The inability of CO2 to effect any conformational change on binding to haemoglobin
II. Changes in oxygen affinity brought about by the binding of 2,3 BPG
III. The tendency to shift from the R to the T form when haemoglobin binds H+
questions.why: Carbon dioxide can bind to terminal amino groups and favour the low-affinity T state. Binding of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and protonation of globin also stabilise the deoxygenated conformation and reduce oxygen affinity.

notes.A: Carbamate formation can influence haemoglobin's T–R equilibrium, so carbon dioxide is not functionally inert.
notes.B: The effect of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate is real, but binding of carbon dioxide can also affect conformation.
notes.D: Protonation favours the T state, but carbon dioxide binding can also alter the equilibrium, and the omitted phosphate is an allosteric effector.
notes.E: The phosphate and proton effects are correct. The denial of a carbon dioxide effect is not.

questions.stem:
The myoglobin and haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curves show that:
I. The myoglobin curve always lies to the right of the haemoglobin curve
II. The haemoglobin curve has a sigmoid shape
III. Myoglobin is more saturated at any given pO2 beyond 0 torrs
questions.why: Myoglobin has the higher oxygen affinity and its hyperbolic curve lies to the left of haemoglobin under typical comparable conditions. Haemoglobin has a sigmoid curve because the tetramer binds oxygen cooperatively.

notes.A: The curve lies to the left: myoglobin reaches a given saturation at a lower partial pressure.
notes.B: The haemoglobin curve is sigmoid, but the myoglobin curve should be placed to its left.
notes.D: Myoglobin's greater saturation at a given physiological oxygen pressure is consistent with a leftward curve, not a rightward one.
notes.E: The curve shape and higher myoglobin saturation are correct. The claimed rightward position reverses the expected comparison.

questions.stem:
The functions of the polypeptide chain in haemoglobin include:
I. prevention of oxidation of haemoglobin
II. creation of a hindered haem environment
III. increasing the affinity of binding of carbon monoxide
questions.why: Globin partly shields haem and forms a pocket that helps limit oxidation of ferrous iron. It also reduces the extreme relative affinity for carbon monoxide seen with free haem and favours reversible oxygen binding.

notes.A: Helping protect ferrous haem is one role. Creating a pocket that restricts ligand access and orientation is another.
notes.C: The globin pocket restricts access, but it decreases the relative carbon monoxide preference compared with free haem.
notes.D: Protection of haem is appropriate. A higher relative carbon monoxide affinity is the opposite of the usual effect of globin.
notes.E: The protection and pocket statements are valid. The claimed increase in carbon monoxide preference is incorrect.

questions.stem:
Some of the functions of the polypeptide chains in haemoglobin include:
I. binding of carbon dioxide
II. buffering of H+
III. binding of oxygen
questions.why: The globin chains bind some carbon dioxide as carbamates and accept protons on ionisable groups. They also hold haem in a pocket that supports reversible oxygen binding. The atom that directly binds oxygen is the haem iron.

notes.A: Carbamate formation is one function. Globin also buffers protons and provides the environment for oxygen binding by haem.
notes.B: Carbon dioxide carriage and proton buffering are valid. The chains also support ligand binding through their association with haem.
notes.C: Proton buffering and support for oxygen binding are important. Amino groups on globin can also carry some carbon dioxide.
notes.D: Globin participates in carbon dioxide and oxygen transport. Its ionisable groups can also accept protons.

questions.stem:
The following statements are true:
I. binding of 2,3 BPG to haemoglobin causes a shift from the T to the R quaternary structure.
II. for any given PO2 beyond zero torr, oxygen saturation is higher for myoglobin than for haemoglobin
III. The binding of CO2 to haemoglobin favours the deoxyhaemoglobin quaternary structure
questions.why: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate preferentially binds the low-affinity T state. Carbon dioxide also favours the deoxygenated conformation. Myoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than haemoglobin under ordinary comparable physiological conditions.

notes.A: The phosphate stabilises the T state, rather than driving a T-to-R transition.
notes.B: The myoglobin affinity comparison is appropriate under typical conditions. The claimed direction of the phosphate effect is reversed.
notes.D: Carbon dioxide can favour deoxyhaemoglobin, but 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate also favours the T state rather than converting it to R.
notes.E: The myoglobin and carbon dioxide statements are appropriate. The claim about a phosphate-induced R state is incorrect.

questions.stem:
The functions of the distal histidine (His E7) in haemoglobin include:
I. Prevention of oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+
II. Encouraging linear binding of CO at the active sites
III. Increasing the affinity of binding of CO to haemoglobin
questions.why: Distal histidine helps shield the haem iron from solvent and stabilises bound oxygen through hydrogen bonding. This can limit auto-oxidation and decreases the strong relative preference for carbon monoxide that is seen with free haem.

notes.B: Protection against oxidation is plausible, but the distal pocket does not promote ideal linear binding of carbon monoxide.
notes.C: The distal environment tends to discriminate against carbon monoxide relative to free haem. Neither of the two carbon monoxide claims describes that protection.
notes.D: The protective role is valid. The pocket does not increase the relative preference for carbon monoxide.
notes.E: The iron-protecting effect is consistent with the haem pocket, but the claims about enhanced carbon monoxide binding are not.

questions.stem:
Haemoglobin S:
I. has a substitution of glutamic acid for valine at position 6 on the β chain
II. has a sticky patch on its surface even when fully oxygenated
III. when deoxygenated has complementary sites that can accommodate the sticky patches
questions.why: In HbS, valine replaces glutamate at position 6 of the β chain (the item's wording 'substitution of glutamic acid for valine' is the lecturer's phrasing for this change). Val-6 forms a hydrophobic 'sticky patch' that is present in both oxy- and deoxy-HbS, but the complementary pocket it fits into appears only on deoxy-HbS, so polymers form when HbS is deoxygenated.

notes.A: Leaves out II and III, which are also true.
notes.B: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.C: Leaves out I, which is also true.
notes.D: Leaves out II, which is also true.

questions.stem:
Concerning haemoglobin S:
I. the sickling of HbS is reversible
II. even when fully oxygenated has complementary sites that can accommodate the sticky patches created by valine at position 6 on the β chain
III. polymerizes by the interaction of sticky patches with complementary sites
questions.why: HbS polymerises when the Val-6 sticky patch of one molecule fits into the complementary site of another (III). Fully oxygenated HbS has no complementary sites (II false). Repeated sickling eventually becomes irreversible, which is why the item treats I as false.

notes.A: Includes I, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.B: Includes I and II, which are false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.C: Includes II, which is false.
notes.D: Includes I, which is false.

questions.stem:
In sickle cell trait:
I. more than 50% of the haemoglobin in the red blood cells is HbS
II. some of the red blood cells have HbA molecules only while other red blood cells carry HbS molecules only
III. both HbS and HbA molecules are present in all the red blood cells
questions.why: In typical sickle cell trait, a person has one normal beta-globin allele and one HbS allele. Erythroid cells express both, so the same red cells generally contain HbA and HbS. HbA usually remains the larger fraction.

notes.A: HbS is usually less than half of total haemoglobin in uncomplicated trait. The ratio can vary with other inherited factors.
notes.B: Trait does not normally produce two separate red cell populations containing only one haemoglobin type. Both globin alleles are expressed within erythroid cells.
notes.C: Coexistence of HbA and HbS is correct, but the proposed separation into two single-type cell populations is not.
notes.D: Both types are normally present within the same cells. HbS does not usually exceed half the total in uncomplicated trait.

questions.stem:
In sickle cell anaemia:
I. Normally no HbF is detected
II. The concentration of HbS is too low for sickling to occur at normal oxygen levels
III. Deoxygenation of the tissues can trigger off a sickling crisis
questions.why: In HbSS, deoxygenation promotes polymerisation of HbS and can contribute to a vaso-occlusive crisis. HbS makes up a large fraction of the haemoglobin, and HbF levels vary between individuals and with treatment.

notes.A: HbF can be present in HbSS. Its amount varies and higher levels can decrease sickling.
notes.B: The HbS fraction is usually high in HbSS. Oxygenated haemoglobin is less prone to polymerise because of its conformation.
notes.C: Deoxygenation can trigger sickling, but this is not explained by an unusually low HbS concentration.
notes.D: Tissue deoxygenation can promote polymerisation. The assertion that HbF is normally absent is incorrect.

questions.stem:
Sickle cell anaemia is:
I. Sickle cell SC disease
II. Sickle cell S-Thalassaemia
III. Sickle cell SS disease
questions.why: In the usual genotype terminology, sickle cell anaemia denotes HbSS, with two HbS alleles. HbSC and HbS–beta-thalassaemia are other forms of sickle cell disease. Some clinical classifications also group HbS–beta-zero thalassaemia with HbSS because their clinical courses can be similar.

notes.B: HbSC and HbS–beta-thalassaemia are recognised sickle cell disease genotypes, but they are not the conventional HbSS designation.
notes.C: HbSS is the classic genotype for sickle cell anaemia. The unqualified beta-thalassaemia label also includes variants with different clinical severity.
notes.D: HbSC is a distinct compound heterozygous genotype. It is not the same as homozygous HbSS.
notes.E: All three can cause sickle cell disease, but they are not interchangeable genotype names.

questions.stem:
Concerning anti-sickling oligopeptides:
I. they work by inhibition of formation of HbS fibers
II. they are synthetic oligopeptides with sequences corresponding to the carboxy-terminal region of the βS chain
III. they work by dissolving HbS crystals
questions.why: They inhibit formation and mimic the C-terminal sequence. They do not dissolve formed crystals.

notes.A: Leaves out II, which is also true.
notes.C: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.D: Includes III, which is false, and leaves out II, which is true.
notes.E: Includes III, which is false.

questions.stem:
Anti-sickling oligopeptides:
I. are being evaluated as polymerization inhibitors of deoxy HbS
II. have a semblance to the 'sticky patch'
III. have a semblance to the 'complementary site'
questions.why: They act as decoys by mimicking the complementary site, not the sticky patch.

notes.A: Leaves out III, which is also true.
notes.B: Includes II, which is false, and leaves out III, which is true.
notes.C: Includes II, which is false, and leaves out I, which is true.
notes.E: Includes II, which is false.

questions.stem:
Anti-sickling isocyanic acid derivatives are:
I. Compounds that increase the oxygenation of haemoglobin S
II. Compounds that increase the oxygen affinity of haemoglobin S
III. Compounds which irreversibly attach to the α-amino groups of haemoglobin S
questions.why: Historical studies examined carbamylation of globin amino termini as a way to increase haemoglobin S oxygen affinity. At the same oxygen pressure this can reduce the deoxygenated fraction available for polymerisation. This is an experimental mechanism rather than standard therapy.

notes.A: A higher oxygenated fraction is a possible consequence, and the change in oxygen affinity and chemical modification also explain it.
notes.B: Increased affinity and oxygenation are related outcomes. Carbamylation of terminal amino groups is the underlying chemical modification.
notes.C: Affinity and carbamylation describe the mechanism. At a given oxygen pressure the higher affinity can increase oxygen saturation.
notes.D: Terminal carbamylation is part of the mechanism. The increased oxygenated fraction follows from the associated increase in affinity.

questions.stem:
The basic defect in the thalassaemias is:
I. synthesis of abnormal haemoglobin polypeptide chains
II. single amino acid substitution in a haemoglobin polypeptide chain
III. reduced production of selected globin chains
questions.why: Thalassaemia is primarily a quantitative disorder of globin synthesis. Reduced production of one chain type leaves an excess of its partner, which can damage developing red cells. A structural amino acid substitution is a different basic mechanism.

notes.A: An abnormal sequence alone describes a structural haemoglobin variant. The defining feature here is inadequate production of a globin chain.
notes.B: Structural defects and point mutations can affect haemoglobin, but thalassaemia is classified by reduced synthesis of a chain.
notes.C: Reduced production is the defining feature. A single amino acid substitution is not required for a thalassaemia phenotype.
notes.D: Some variants change both structure and expression, but an abnormal polypeptide is not the defining defect of all thalassaemias.

questions.stem:
The thalassaemias can be caused by:
I. mismatch in the rate of synthesis of α and β polypeptide chains
II. polymerization of deoxy-haemoglobins
III. precipitation of haem in immature red blood cells
questions.why: In thalassaemia, reduced synthesis of one globin chain class produces an imbalance between alpha and beta-type chains. Excess unpaired globin can precipitate and damage erythroid cells. This differs from deoxyhaemoglobin S polymerisation.

notes.B: Polymerisation of deoxyhaemoglobin is characteristic of sickle haemoglobin. The imbalance in globin synthesis is the thalassaemic defect.
notes.C: Neither deoxyhaemoglobin polymerisation nor precipitation of free haem defines thalassaemia. Unpaired globin chains are the important precipitating material.
notes.D: Chain imbalance is correct, but the precipitates contain excess unpaired globin rather than free haem as the primary lesion.
notes.E: The synthesis mismatch is correct. The other statements confuse it with HbS polymerisation or with precipitation of haem rather than globin.

questions.stem: True or false: The total complement of alpha genes in an individual is four.
questions.why: The usual alpha-globin complement is four genes. Each copy of chromosome 16 normally carries HBA1 and HBA2, so two chromosomes provide four functioning copies in the ordinary genotype.

notes.B: Gene deletions or duplications can change the number, but a typical diploid alpha-globin genotype has four copies.

questions.stem: True or false: Silent carrier alpha thalassemia genotype is: -a/aa
questions.why: A silent alpha-thalassaemia carrier commonly has one nonfunctioning alpha-globin gene and three functional copies. This is conventionally represented as −α/αα.

notes.B: The displayed genotype represents loss of one gene on one chromosome, leaving three functional alpha-globin genes.

questions.stem: True or false: Minor alpha thalassemia genotype is: -a/-a, -/aa
questions.why: Alpha-thalassaemia trait typically involves two affected alpha-globin genes. The changes may be in trans, one on each chromosome, or in cis, both on the same chromosome.

notes.B: The two usual deletion patterns are −α/−α and −−/αα, so the shorthand describes two ways to lose two functional copies.

questions.stem: True or false: Hb H disease genotype is: -/-a
questions.why: Haemoglobin H disease usually involves loss or inactivation of three alpha-globin genes. The usual deletion genotype is −−/−α. Excess beta chains can associate into beta-four tetramers, called HbH.

notes.B: When the dash stands for an alpha-zero chromosome, the displayed combination leaves only one functional alpha-globin gene.

questions.stem: True or false: Barts hydrops fetalis genotype is: -/-
questions.why: The classic haemoglobin Bart hydrops fetalis syndrome results from loss of all four alpha-globin genes, conventionally written −−/−−. Excess fetal gamma chains form gamma-four tetramers with very high oxygen affinity.

notes.B: The shorthand refers to both chromosomes lacking functional alpha-globin genes, rather than to a one-gene deletion on each.

questions.stem: The following is true about the distribution of amino-acids in myoglobin:

options.label: A
options.text: The interior of myoglobin does not have any polar amino acids at all

options.label: B
options.text: The interior of myoglobin consists of only non-polar amino-acids

options.label: C
options.text: The interior of myoglobin consists of residues such as leucine, valine, methionine, and phenylalanine

options.label: D
options.text: Side chains of glutamate, aspartate, glutamine, asparagine, lysine or arginine are abundant in the interior of myoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: Residues that have both a polar and a non-polar part are positioned such that their non-polar part points inward

notes.A: The core is not wholly nonpolar. Histidines associated with the ligand-binding pocket have polar side chains.
notes.B: Hydrophobic packing predominates, but the haem pocket includes polar residues needed for function.
notes.C: Leucine, valine, methionine and phenylalanine are examples of residues that can contribute to hydrophobic packing within a globin fold.
notes.D: Many charged or strongly polar side chains are exposed to solvent, rather than abundant in the buried core.
notes.E: Amphipathic side chains can pack nonpolar portions inward while exposing their polar groups, depending on their local environment.

questions.why: Myoglobin has a largely hydrophobic core that encloses haem, while many charged or polar groups face the solvent. The core still contains important polar residues, notably the histidines associated with the haem pocket.

questions.stem: The oxygen binding site in haemoglobin:

options.label: A
options.text: Is the co-ordination position of the distal histidine

options.label: B
options.text: Is the co-ordination position of the proximal histidine

options.label: C
options.text: Does not function properly if the haem iron is in the +2 oxidation state

options.label: D
options.text: Does not function properly if the haem iron is in the +3 oxidation state

notes.A: The distal histidine lies near the ligand but does not occupy the oxygen-binding coordination position.
notes.B: The proximal histidine binds the fifth position of iron, on the side opposite the oxygen ligand.
notes.C: Ferrous iron is the oxidation state required for normal reversible oxygen binding.
notes.D: Ferric iron gives methaemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen normally at the affected haem site.
notes.E: Carbon dioxide can form carbamates with globin amino groups. It does not use the oxygen-binding coordination position of iron.

questions.why: Oxygen binds directly to ferrous haem iron at its sixth coordination position. The proximal histidine coordinates the fifth position, while the distal histidine helps shape the ligand pocket. Oxidation to ferric iron prevents normal reversible oxygen binding.

questions.stem: The following are interactions that take place at the active sites of haem or haemoglobin:

options.label: A
options.text: Oxygen binds to the iron atom in haem

options.label: B
options.text: Free haem in aqueous solution binds oxygen reversibly for a very short time

options.label: C
options.text: Free haem is rapidly oxidised to methaem

options.label: E
options.text: With free haem, a haem-oxygen-haem complex is formed before the formation of methaem

notes.A: The oxygen ligand coordinates the ferrous iron atom in the haem group.
notes.B: Free ferrous haem can interact transiently with oxygen, but rapid oxidation limits sustained reversible binding in aqueous solution.
notes.C: Removal of the protective globin environment makes ferric haem formation much more likely on exposure to oxygen.
notes.D: Ferric haem cannot bind and release oxygen in the normal reversible way used by ferrous haemoglobin.
notes.E: In classical models of free-haem auto-oxidation, oxygen-derived bridges can form between haem groups before ferric products accumulate.

questions.why: Oxygen interacts with ferrous haem iron. In unprotected aqueous systems, free haem can auto-oxidise rapidly and form bridged products. Globin restrains these reactions and makes oxygen binding reliably reversible in haemoglobin.

questions.stem: Interactions at the active sites of haemoglobin:

options.label: A
options.text: The distal histidine, histidine E7 and other residues surrounding the sixth coordination point cause the formation of haem-oxygen-haem complexes

options.label: B
options.text: Residues surrounding the sixth co-ordination point prevent oxidation of the haem iron

options.label: C
options.text: Residues surrounding the sixth co-ordination point stabilize the ferrous form of haemoglobin

options.label: D
options.text: The polypeptide chain creates a hindered haem environment which allows haem to reversibly bind oxygen for long periods of time

options.label: E
options.text: The polypeptide chain creates an enhanced haem environment which allows haem to reversibly bind oxygen for long periods of time

notes.A: They prevent this complex formation by steric hindrance.
notes.B: The hydrophobic pocket protects the iron.
notes.D: The steric hindrance prevents irreversible oxidation.
notes.E: It creates a hindered environment, not enhanced.
notes.C: The hydrophobic pocket keeps iron as Fe2+.

questions.why: The globin chain gives haem a hindered, hydrophobic pocket around the sixth position that stops haem–O₂–haem complexes and keeps the iron ferrous, so O₂ binds reversibly.

questions.stem: The following statements about haemoglobin quaternary structure are true:

options.label: A
options.text: The α1β2 interface is closely connected to the haem

options.label: B
options.text: The α1β2 interface is supposed to be the functional contact area of haemoglobin

options.label: C
options.text: Large structural changes take place at the α1β2 interface on oxygenation

options.label: D
options.text: The α1β1 interface is a relatively fixed (stabilizing) contact area

options.label: E
options.text: A number of salt linkages are broken in the α1β1 interface on oxygenation

notes.A: The α1β1 interface is closer to the heme.
notes.B: It slides significantly during oxygenation.
notes.E: Salt linkages break at the α1β2 interface.
notes.C: Oxygenation shifts the α1β2 contact (T to R).
notes.D: The α1β1 contact barely changes.

questions.why: The α1β1 contact is a fixed, stabilising interface, while the α1β2 contact is the functional one where salt links break and the dimers slide as haemoglobin shifts from T to R.

questions.stem: The term sickle cell disease includes:

notes.A: HbSC disease arises when an HbS allele is inherited with an HbC allele and can produce sickling complications.
notes.B: Combining HbS with a beta-thalassaemia allele can cause sickle cell disease, with severity depending on the partner allele.
notes.C: In HbSS, a person inherits two HbS alleles. This is the classic genotype of sickle cell anaemia.
notes.D: HbAS usually denotes sickle cell trait, with one normal beta-globin allele alongside HbS.
notes.E: HbAC commonly denotes HbC trait and does not include the HbS allele required for a sickling disorder.

questions.why: Sickle cell disease includes genotypes in which HbS is inherited with another beta-globin allele that produces a disease phenotype. Common examples include HbSS, HbSC and HbS–beta-thalassaemia. HbAS usually denotes trait.

questions.stem: The vicious cycle of sickling involves:

options.label: A
options.text: Distortion of red cell shape by polymerized HbS

notes.A: Intracellular HbS fibres deform red cells and make them less flexible.
notes.B: Less deformable cells, endothelial adhesion and other vascular factors can obstruct small blood vessels.
notes.C: Obstruction reduces local perfusion and oxygen delivery, making the local environment more favourable to sickling.
notes.D: Lower oxygen tension favours more deoxy-HbS polymerisation, reinforcing the obstruction–hypoxia cycle.
notes.E: Repeated deformation damages the membrane and shortens red-cell survival, contributing to haemolysis alongside vaso-occlusion.

questions.why: Deoxygenation favours HbS polymer formation and distortion of red cells. Rigid cells can obstruct small vessels, reducing local oxygen delivery and promoting further polymerisation. Repeated cellular injury also causes haemolysis.

questions.stem: Concerning anti-sickling oligopeptides:

options.label: A
options.text: They work by dissolving formed HbS fibers

options.label: B
options.text: They are synthetic oligopeptides with sequences corresponding to the carboxylterminal region of the βS chain

options.label: C
options.text: They are stereo-specific gelation inhibitors of HbS

options.label: E
options.text: They resemble the 'complementary sites' which develop on deoxyhaemoglobin A or S

notes.A: They prevent formation.
notes.D: They resemble the complementary site.
notes.B: They copy the region of βS that makes contacts in the polymer.
notes.C: They specifically block polymer (gel) formation.
notes.E: They block the acceptor sites to which the sticky patch binds.

questions.why: Anti-sickling oligopeptides are synthetic stereospecific inhibitors that mimic the complementary acceptor sites on deoxy-Hb, so the sticky patch cannot bind and HbS fibres do not form.

questions.stem: Isocyanic acid anti-sickling derivatives include:

options.label: A
options.text: Compounds that decrease the concentration of deoxy-haemoglobin S

options.label: B
options.text: Compounds that increase the oxygen affinity of haemoglobin S

options.label: C
options.text: Cyanate which enters red blood cells and irreversibly carbamylates the α-amino groups of haemoglobin

notes.A: Increasing affinity can lower the deoxygenated fraction at the same oxygen pressure, reducing the form that polymerises.
notes.B: Terminal carbamylation changes haemoglobin's oxygen-binding behaviour and can favour oxygenated states.
notes.C: Cyanate can carbamylate terminal alpha-amino groups, forming a stable covalent modification that affects oxygen affinity.

questions.why: Historical cyanate studies used terminal carbamylation of haemoglobin to increase oxygen affinity. At a given oxygen tension, that leaves less deoxygenated HbS available to polymerise. This mechanism did not establish cyanate as routine treatment.

questions.stem: Anti-sickling ion channel-active drugs are:

options.label: A
options.text: Drugs that cause a decrease in the total concentration of haemoglobin S in the red cell through red cell volume changes

options.label: B
options.text: Drugs that increase the total concentration of haemoglobin F in the red cell

options.label: C
options.text: Agents that increase the volume of the red cell

options.label: D
options.text: Agents that decrease the volume of the red cell

options.label: E
options.text: Agents that affect ion pumps and channels in the red blood cell membrane

notes.A: Preserving water can reduce the intracellular concentration of HbS, even though the number of HbS molecules in the cell need not change.
notes.B: Raising HbF is a different therapeutic mechanism involving globin expression. It is not the direct result of inhibiting a dehydration pathway.
notes.C: Preserving or increasing cell water relative to a dehydrated state lowers the concentration of haemoglobin inside the cell.
notes.D: Losing cell water concentrates HbS and favours polymerisation, rather than producing the desired dilution.
notes.E: Red-cell ion channels and transporters influence water balance, so they can be studied as targets for reducing dehydration.

questions.why: Red-cell dehydration increases intracellular HbS concentration and promotes polymerisation. Ion transport interventions can try to preserve cell water and lower HbS concentration by dilution, without changing the amount of globin made.

questions.stem: New approaches to therapy of sickle cell disease include:

options.label: A
options.text: Activation of HbF synthesis using hydroxyurea, 5-azacytidine, decytabine

options.label: B
options.text: Antisickling agents acting on hemoglobin or red cell membrane

options.label: E
options.text: Administration of oxygen, intravenous fluids and analgesics

notes.A: These drugs switch on γ-globin, raising HbF.
notes.B: These agents act on Hb or the red cell membrane.
notes.C: A transplant can cure the disease.
notes.D: Gene therapy is an emerging cure.
notes.E: These are core supportive treatments for crises.

questions.why: Therapy combines supportive care (oxygen, fluids, analgesia) with newer approaches: raising HbF (hydroxyurea), anti-sickling agents, bone marrow transplant and gene therapy.

questions.stem: The basic defects in the thalassaemias include:

options.label: A
options.text: Synthesis of abnormal haemoglobin polypeptide chains

options.label: B
options.text: Single amino acid substitution in a haemoglobin polypeptide chain

options.label: C
options.text: Reduced production of selected globin chains

options.label: D
options.text: Mismatch in the rate of synthesis of α and β polypeptide chains

options.label: E
options.text: Precipitation of globin chains in immature red blood cells

notes.A: A structurally abnormal globin can cause a haemoglobinopathy, but thalassaemia is primarily defined by reduced chain output.
notes.B: A single amino acid change can produce a structural variant. It is not a necessary feature of thalassaemia.
notes.C: Lower production of a specific chain class is the primary defect in alpha- or beta-thalassaemia.
notes.D: The affected chain is produced more slowly or not at all, so its partner can accumulate in excess.
notes.E: Some excess unpaired chains precipitate in developing red cells, damaging those cells and contributing to ineffective erythropoiesis.

questions.why: Thalassaemia is defined by reduced production of selected globin chains. The resulting imbalance can leave unpaired chains that precipitate in erythroid precursors and contribute to ineffective erythropoiesis. Precipitation is a downstream mechanism of injury.

questions.stem: The thalassaemias result from:

options.label: A
options.text: Deletion or malfunction of genes located on chromosomes 11 and 16

options.label: C
options.text: Instability of the mRNA directing globin chain synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Instability of the globin chain itself

options.label: E
options.text: Reduced production of selected globin chains

notes.A: The alpha-globin genes are on chromosome 16 and the beta-globin gene is on chromosome 11. Loss or dysfunction can reduce the relevant chain output.
notes.B: Variants can impair transcription, RNA processing or translation, leaving less functional globin.
notes.C: Some variants produce unstable transcripts or trigger transcript decay, so less globin is made.
notes.D: Some unusually unstable globin variants are degraded rapidly and can produce a thalassaemic phenotype. This is not the usual mechanism of every form.
notes.E: A decrease in one globin chain type is the defining quantitative change and leaves an imbalance with its partner chain.

questions.why: Alpha- and beta-thalassaemia reduce the output of one globin chain type. Deletions, regulatory variants, abnormal RNA processing and unstable globin products are different ways an affected gene can reduce the amount of usable globin.

questions.stem: Recognized forms of beta thalassaemia include:

notes.A: Two normal β genes.
notes.B: One affected β gene gives the minor (trait) form.
notes.C: Two β+ genes leave some β chain production.
notes.D: No or very little β chain is made.

questions.why: β-thalassaemia severity follows how much β chain the two genes make: one affected gene gives minor (trait), two β⁺ genes intermedia, and β⁰ with β⁰ or β⁺ major.

questions.stem: The following statements about the thalassaemias are true:

options.label: A
options.text: The total complement of alpha genes in an individual is four

options.label: B
options.text: The total complement of alpha genes in an individual is two

options.label: C
options.text: Beta thalassaemia is usually caused by gene deletion

options.label: D
options.text: Alpha thalassaemia is usually caused by gene deletion

options.label: E
options.text: The main problem in thalassaemia is a mismatch of the rate of synthesis of α and β globin chains

notes.A: Each chromosome 16 usually carries HBA1 and HBA2, giving four alpha-globin genes in the typical diploid complement.
notes.B: Two functional alpha-globin genes can occur in alpha-thalassaemia trait. The usual complement is four.
notes.C: Most beta-thalassaemia alleles are point variants or small sequence changes that alter expression or processing. Larger deletions are less common.
notes.D: Deletions that remove one or more alpha-globin genes are a common cause of alpha-thalassaemia.
notes.E: Reduced synthesis of one chain class leaves excess unpaired partner chains, contributing to red-cell injury.

questions.why: A typical person has four functional alpha-globin genes. Alpha-thalassaemia commonly results from deletions, whereas beta-thalassaemia more often involves sequence variants that reduce expression. The shared consequence is unbalanced production of globin chains.

questions.stem: Genotypic forms of alpha thalassaemia are as follows:

notes.A: The displayed pattern lacks one functional alpha-globin gene. The ordinary genotype has two functioning genes on each chromosome.
notes.B: Loss of one alpha-globin copy leaves three functional genes and is often clinically silent.
notes.C: Two affected genes can be on opposite chromosomes or on the same chromosome. These are the usual trans and cis forms of the trait.
notes.D: With three genes affected, excess beta chains can form HbH, a beta-four tetramer.
notes.E: Loss of all four genes allows excess fetal gamma chains to form haemoglobin Bart and produces severe fetal disease.

questions.why: The usual alpha-globin genotype has four functional copies. One affected copy gives silent carrier status, two give alpha-thalassaemia trait, three usually give HbH disease, and loss of all four gives classic haemoglobin Bart hydrops fetalis.

questions.stem: Haemoglobin Properties (HbF and adult HbA):

options.label: B
options.text: Foetal haemoglobin (HbF) has the same affinity for 2,3-BPG as HbA

options.label: C
options.text: Position 143γ in foetal haemoglobin is serine

options.label: D
options.text: Position 143γ in foetal haemoglobin is histidine

options.label: E
options.text: Position 143β in adult haemoglobin A is histidine

notes.A: Myoglobin is a monomer with one haem group. Its oxygen binding is not cooperative.
notes.B: HbF binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate less strongly than HbA, contributing to its higher oxygen affinity.
notes.C: Serine occupies gamma-chain position 143 and does not supply the same positive interaction as adult beta-chain histidine.
notes.D: Position 143 of the fetal gamma chain is serine, while histidine is found at the homologous adult beta-chain position.
notes.E: Adult beta globin has histidine at position 143, contributing to interactions in the 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binding pocket.

questions.why: Fetal haemoglobin contains gamma chains in place of adult beta chains. The gamma-chain serine at position 143 contributes to less binding of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which helps give HbF a higher oxygen affinity than HbA.

questions.stem: The allosteric manifestations of haemoglobin include:

options.label: B
options.text: The sigmoidal nature of the haemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve

options.label: C
options.text: Conformational changes in structure brought about by a lowering of pH

options.label: D
options.text: The inability of a sharp increase in [CO2] to effect any conformational change in haemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: Changes in oxygen affinity brought about by the binding of 2,3 BPG

notes.A: Oxygen binding at one site increases the tendency of other subunits to bind oxygen.
notes.B: Positive cooperativity gives the haemoglobin saturation curve its sigmoid shape.
notes.C: Increased proton concentration favours the low-affinity T state, contributing to the Bohr effect.
notes.D: Carbon dioxide can form carbamates and affect the T–R equilibrium. It can also lower pH through hydration reactions.
notes.E: The phosphate binds preferentially to the deoxygenated tetramer and reduces its affinity for oxygen.

questions.why: Haemoglobin's subunits communicate through changes in quaternary structure. Oxygen binding increases affinity at other subunits, while increased protons, carbon dioxide and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate favour lower-affinity conformations.

questions.stem: The oxygen dissociation curves for myoglobin and haemoglobin show that:

options.label: A
options.text: Myoglobin is more saturated with oxygen at any given PO2

options.label: B
options.text: The myoglobin curve always lies to the right of the haemoglobin curve

options.label: C
options.text: The haemoglobin curve has a sigmoid shape

options.label: D
options.text: The P50 of haemoglobin is 26 torrs

options.label: E
options.text: The P50 of myoglobin is 16 torrs

notes.A: At the same typical physiological oxygen pressure, the higher-affinity myoglobin is generally more saturated.
notes.B: The myoglobin curve is displaced toward lower oxygen pressures and therefore lies to the left.
notes.C: Communication between haemoglobin subunits during oxygen binding produces a sigmoidal curve.
notes.D: A P50 near 26 torr is a standard adult haemoglobin estimate. The value varies with pH, temperature and other factors.
notes.E: Myoglobin's P50 is much lower than 16 torr, typically around two to three torr in standard teaching comparisons.

questions.why: Myoglobin has a hyperbolic oxygen saturation curve and reaches half saturation at a lower oxygen pressure than haemoglobin. Adult haemoglobin has a sigmoid curve and a P50 around 26–27 torr under standard physiological conditions.

questions.stem: The functions of the polypeptide chain in haemoglobin include:

options.label: A
options.text: Prevention of oxidation of active site Fe2+ to Fe3+

options.label: B
options.text: Decreasing the affinity of binding of carbon monoxide

notes.A: The protein environment helps limit auto-oxidation of ferrous haem, although some ferric methaemoglobin can still form.
notes.B: The distal environment reduces the relative carbon monoxide preference compared with free haem and supports oxygen binding.
notes.C: Ionisable groups in globin can take up hydrogen ions and help buffer the blood.
notes.D: Globin positions and protects the haem for oxygen binding. The oxygen molecule directly coordinates the haem iron.
notes.E: 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate binds in a cavity between the beta chains, preferentially in the deoxygenated conformation.

questions.why: Globin supplies a pocket that protects haem and supports reversible oxygen binding. It reduces the extreme carbon monoxide preference seen with free haem, accepts protons and provides an allosteric binding site for 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

questions.stem: True or false: The total complement of alpha genes in an individual is two.
questions.why: A typical diploid genome contains four alpha-globin genes. Each of the two chromosome 16 copies carries HBA1 and HBA2, although variants can alter the number.

notes.A: Two genes per chromosome does not mean two in total. With two chromosome copies, the usual whole-genome count is four.

questions.stem: True or false: Beta thalassaemia is usually caused by gene deletion.
questions.why: Beta-thalassaemia usually results from variants that affect beta-globin transcription, RNA splicing, RNA stability or translation. Gene deletions are possible, but they account for a smaller proportion than nondeletion variants.

notes.A: Large gene deletions can cause beta-thalassaemia, but most cases are due to other sequence changes that reduce beta-globin production.

questions.stem: True or false: Alpha thalassaemia is usually caused by gene deletion.
questions.why: Alpha-thalassaemia commonly results when a chromosomal deletion removes one or more alpha-globin genes. Some nondeletion variants also reduce alpha-globin function or output.

notes.B: Nondeletion forms exist, but loss of alpha-globin genes by deletion is a common mechanism and supports the statement.

questions.stem: True or false: The main problem in thalassaemia is a mismatch of the rate of synthesis of α and β globin chains.
questions.why: In thalassaemia, one class of globin is made in reduced amounts. Unpaired partner chains then accumulate relative to the affected chain, harming erythroid precursors or mature red cells.

notes.B: The chain imbalance is central to disease even though the particular gene and degree of deficiency differ among forms.

questions.stem: True or false: Normal alpha thalassemia genotype is: -a/aa.
questions.why: A typical alpha-globin genotype has two functioning genes on each chromosome 16, written αα/αα. The displayed genotype lacks one copy and is usually the silent carrier pattern.

notes.A: The deletion indicator leaves only three functional genes overall, so the pattern is not the usual four-gene genotype.

questions.stem: Functions of Platelets in Coagulation

options.label: A
options.text: They provide anchorage for activation of some clotting factors

options.label: C
options.text: They concentrate the clotting factors by as much as 10^4 times

options.label: D
options.text: The disrupted platelet lipid surfaces ensure that the accelerated reactions will occur far from the site of injury

options.label: E
options.text: They chelate calcium and make it unavailable for the clotting process

notes.A: Platelets provide a phospholipid surface.
notes.B: They concentrate them.
notes.C: Platelets concentrate clotting factors locally.
notes.D: They occur exactly at the site of injury.
notes.E: Platelets provide calcium; EDTA and citrate chelate it.

questions.why: Activated platelets expose a phospholipid surface that anchors and concentrates clotting factors (up to about 10⁴-fold), keeping the reactions fast and confined to the site of injury.

questions.stem: Properties of Fibrinopeptides

options.label: A
options.text: Have a large net negative charge on their surface

options.label: B
options.text: Have an abundance of uncharged amino-acids

options.label: C
options.text: Have an abundance of negatively charged amino-acids on their surface

notes.C: This prevents premature aggregation.
notes.D: Fibrinopeptide B contains this.
notes.E: Γ-carboxyglutamates are in clotting factors, not fibrinopeptides.
notes.A: Acidic residues give a strong negative charge, so the peptides repel.
notes.B: They are rich in CHARGED (acidic) residues.

questions.why: Fibrinopeptides A and B carry many acidic residues (and B has tyrosine-O-sulfate), so their strong negative charge keeps fibrinogen molecules apart until thrombin removes them.

questions.stem: Anticoagulant Agents

notes.A: Oxalate precipitates calcium.
notes.B: Citrate is an anticoagulant.
notes.D: Warfarin is an antagonist.
notes.C: EDTA removes Ca2+, which clotting needs.
notes.E: Coumarins block vitamin K recycling.

questions.why: Citrate, oxalate and EDTA prevent clotting in vitro by removing Ca²⁺, while warfarin and other coumarins act in vivo as vitamin K antagonists.

questions.stem: Haemophilia

options.label: A
options.text: Is transmitted as a sex-linked recessive characteristic

options.label: B
options.text: Is transmitted as an autosomal dominant characteristic

options.label: C
options.text: Is caused by a deficiency of factor VIII

options.label: D
options.text: Is caused by a deficiency of factor IX

options.label: E
options.text: Has the same clinical picture as deficiency of Christmas factor

notes.A: The common inherited forms result from F8 or F9 variants on the X chromosome, with the usual X-linked recessive pattern.
notes.B: The classic inheritance of haemophilia A and B is X-linked, rather than autosomal dominant.
notes.C: Deficient factor VIII activity defines haemophilia A. It impairs efficient assembly or function of the intrinsic tenase complex.
notes.D: Deficient factor IX activity defines haemophilia B. The resulting bleeding pattern can resemble haemophilia A.
notes.E: Christmas factor is factor IX. Patients with its deficiency can have a clinical bleeding pattern similar to that seen in factor VIII deficiency.

questions.why: Haemophilia A is due to factor VIII deficiency and haemophilia B to factor IX deficiency. Both are usually X-linked recessive and can produce similar bleeding patterns. Haemophilia B is also called Christmas disease.
